Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to bring the Canadian Immigration Act up to date with current opinion in Canada and in the world but in which Canada may be a world leader.
In the past the immigration laws of the United Nations and of Canada reflected mainly the situation of men who were engaged in political activity or were religious leaders and were persecuted. Now it is becoming evident that women in some cases are persecuted because they are women.
This bill amends our Immigration Act so that it adds a sixth ground of recognized persecution. In addition to race, nationality, religion, membership in a particular group or political opinion, it would now read that a person may be found a refugee by reason of a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, sex, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion.

They are drawing the attention of Parliament to the following: that the majority of Canadians support equal treatment of criminal offenders but with legislated aid shelters from criminal law for very young adolescents and that chapter 15 of the charter of rights guarantees equality rights.
Therefore these thousands of petitioners-and there are more to come on behalf of this family who is mourning-are requesting that Parliament revise the laws of Canada to replace the Young Offenders Act with an updated Juvenile Delinquents Act with a lowered maximum age of 13 years.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I moved the adjournment of the budget debate yesterday I described this budget as a white flag being raised by all the members of a tired Conservative government in
surrender to a jobless recovery, a jobless economy. Perhaps I should have called the budget this government's shroud because this is surely the last will and testament of a dying government.
In this budget there is nothing for the unemployed, nothing for our young people entering the labour force hoping for a future. In fact the Minister of Finance is projecting unemployment at or near to 11 per cent well into 1994, a message of despair for the 1.5 unemployed Canadians and their families.
On page 21 of the budget papers themselves the Minister of Finance admits that unemployment will be high right through 1998, five years from now. Here is what the budget papers say:
The medium-term projection underlying the fiscal plan is based on
the assumption that some excess capacity in labour and product
markets will remain through 1998.
Underneath this convoluted Department of Finance language the meaning is clear. There still will not be enough jobs five years from now for Canadians if this Conservative government stays in office, but I am sure this is not something Canadians will allow to happen.
Before he brought down his budget the Minister of Finance in effect admitted that putting Canadians back to work would not be his primary focus. He claimed that the deficit was his number one economic enemy.
Canadians are going to think that sounds rather strange coming from this Conservative government. Is this not the same government that said when it was first elected in 1984 that the deficit would be its priority? Is this not the same Conservative government that for the last nine years brought in deficit after deficit all in the $30 billion area? Is this not the same government that over these same nine years piled up more public debt than all previous governments since Confederation? I think so, Mr. Speaker, because there was an accumulated debt of $168 billion approximately by 1984, accumulated in the 117 years since Confederation. However, in only nine years of Conservative government, of Conservative fiscal mismanagement, that debt ballooned to $458 billion. Yet the Conservatives are the people who say they know how to run this country's affairs.

What a laugh, someone said. Canadians have tragically learned that is not the case.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
Even after bragging last week about how his budget was going to fight the deficit, the minister when presenting his budget papers was still forecasting in them that the deficit would be $35.5 billion this year.
Even after five more years under his so-called deficit reduction plan the minister says there would still be a deficit left of $8 billion. Over that same period he plans, the Conservatives plan, to add over $100 billion more to the public debt bringing it to $563.2 billion by 1998.
Under this Conservative government more and more of Canada's debt is held by foreigners leaving us increasingly vulnerable to outside pressures. The government knows this. On page 26 of the budget the Minister of Finance admits that Canada's foreign indebtedness has not been as high since 1961. As I said last night, that was during the last period of long-term Conservative government when the Prime Minister was the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker.
When I pointed that out yesterday our present Conservative Prime Minister doubted this could be so, but here it is in black and white, right here in the Conservative budget and budget papers. This Conservative government and the present Prime Minister have beaten the record of the last Conservative government to the detriment of the Canadian people.
In fact the deficit for 1992-93 is $8 billion higher than this Minister of Finance said it would be in his February 1992 budget and $1.1 billion higher than he said it would be only last December in his economic statement. These guys really know how to forecast. Is that sound fiscal management? I do not think so and Canadians will not think so either.
I am sure that no Conservative members will be as disappointed with this Conservative deficit non-plan than the Minister of National Defence who said she could eliminate the deficit entirely in five years and the Minister of the Environment who then upped the ante saying that he could do it in only four years.
How are these ministers going to reconcile their leadership campaign promises with the Minister of Finance's budget? Will they vote against it because it does not meet these leadership promises? Or will they
vote for it and acknowledge when it comes to fiscal realism they do not know what they are talking about? After all that is what the Minister of Finance in effect said himself about these two colleagues when he forecast yesterday a budget deficit of $8 billion, not zero but $8 billion five years from now.
If this budget is not believable when it comes to deficit control, exactly what does it do? Well it certainly does not set priorities. The Minister of Finance who wants to be known as "Maz the Knife" has said he is four square behind spending $5.8 billion on unneeded high-tech military helicopters which were planned for during a cold war that fortunately ended years ago.
His plan and the Conservative government's commitment is to spend this $5.8 billion at a time when in this budget the government is cutting funds for social housing, for low-income housing, for regional development and is even taking away the January GST rebate cheques from lower income Canadians.
Why is it that after all the talk, the hype, the sales pitches, the Conservatives have failed by their own admission to meet their own objective and bring the deficit under control? It is because they just do not get it. They fail to recognize that meaningful deficit reduction can only be expected when there is strong economic growth and strong increasing employment.
The Minister of Finance and the Conservatives admitted in the budget that government revenues have been weak and would continue to be weak for years under their projections. Why is this? It is because of a continuing weak economy and slow economic growth. The Tories have failed to realize that the deficit, employment, economic growth, inflation and taxation are all interrelated. What is required is a set of co-ordinated and balanced economic policies.
This is exactly what the Conservatives have not given Canadians over the past nine years. There is no doubt the deficit is a problem that must be dealt with. However, any fiscally responsible economic strategy must have two tracks. This is the Liberal approach, the Liberal plan.
The first track involves expenditure control through streamlining government and eliminating duplication while delivering the services that Canadians need. This
April 27, 1993

must take place, we believe, in consultation and not in conflict with the provinces. In addition, the federal government must hold off on new programs that do not contribute to economic growth and job creation.
On the second track at the same time governments must foster economic growth and job creation. This means investing in people, research and development and infrastructure. When people are working it means higher government revenues without their having to pay higher taxes. At the same time governments do not have to spend on unemployment insurance and welfare.
Studies have confirmed that the one million Canadians who are unemployed cost the federal government more than $20 billion, likely $25 billion each and every year they remain out of work. If one million Canadians could be put back to work, it would free up $25 billion which could be directed to other productive purposes. This means these people would be put back to work. That is something for which the Conservatives have no plan. It is something for which the Conservatives have no commitment.
People often ask what government spending we Liberals would like to cut. By way of example, I have already mentioned the $5.8 billion military helicopter program. That is one area. I would also like to see a substantial cut in the $19 billion the government spends on unemployment insurance, not by cutting benefits but by putting people back to work.
Someone once said that to govern is to choose, but this Conservative government has a mania for making bad choices. For example, the Conservatives have no plan for jobs and growth. However, they do have a detailed plan for a multimillion dollar unnecessary farewell trip to Europe by the current Prime Minister. The Conservatives announced no plan for growth and jobs, but the Prime Minister's office has just announced all the details, the full agenda for the multimillion dollar farewell trip by the Prime Minister.
The egomania of the Prime Minister is more important than jobs for Canadians. Surely that cannot be right. Canadians can and will make sure that the next election will also be the farewell trip for the new Conservative leader and the Conservative government as well. We are going to have two farewell trips, one by the present Prime Minister and during the next election the farewell trip for his successor as well.
The Budget
In my own city of Windsor and in cities just like it across this country, people have been devastated by Conservative policies that have brought recession and unemployment. Policies like the GST and the trade deals have closed factories and produced hundreds of thousands of bankruptcies.
People in my community feel they have done more than their share in bearing the burden of these Conservative policies. I think people in my community and communities like it right across this country would be prepared to do their share as part of a plan to help get this country moving. However they see no such plan for recovery and growth in this budget or in anything the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister, or those hoping to succeed him, have had to say so far or are likely to say.
In the budget documents the government admits that even in 1998, five years from now, if there is still a Conservative government it expects to be spending $18 billion a year on unemployment insurance. That is only about $1 billion less than it is spending today. That is hardly a vote of confidence by this Conservative government in its own capacity for economic management.
As the Leader of the Opposition told Toronto's Empire Club on February 11 of this year, fostering economic growth does not mean new federal spending to finance our future. It does mean changing priorities and investing in that future. Without the Liberal two-track approach to deficit reduction and economic growth, any efforts to balance expenditures and revenues will prove futile at best and counterproductive at worst. Meanwhile the stagnant economy will continue. It will continue unless this two-track approach becomes the foundation of a new economic plan for Canada.
The fact is that neither this budget nor any of the Conservative leadership candidates have provided a realistic vision, a plan to achieve the twin objectives of fiscal responsibility and strong economic growth.

Unlike the Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party, the Liberal Party developed an economic policy which will really prepare the Canadian economy for the 21st century.

April 27, 1993

The Budget

For Liberals the ultimate objective of economic policy is to build a value-added economy that will create permanent jobs for Canadians and protect and enhance our social fabric. This means providing Canadians with more jobs with a future in industries with a future.
To maintain high-paying jobs in the global economy Canada will need a work force second to none in skills and flexibility. In co-operation with the provinces, business and labour a new Liberal government would establish a national apprenticeship program and a Canada youth service, for example.
A new Liberal government would see technological innovation as a real opportunity for Canadians. It would pursue a research and development strategy that would enhance Canada's ability to finance, market, administer and diffuse our advanced technology.
A new Liberal government would revitalize the small business sector which is crucial to Canada's long-term economic health. It is this sector that will likely generate the most jobs for Canadians.
A new Liberal government would promote and pursue a global trade strategy and aggressively exploit the potential for export sales to growth areas such as the Pacific rim and Latin America.
A new Liberal government is committed to the concept of a true Canadian economic union, one that would eliminate provincial barriers to the movement of goods, services, capital and labour and create billions of dollars of additional economic activity for Canadians.
Liberals believe that with a national government that stands up for them Canadians can compete with the best in the world, creating new economic growth and opportunity here at home.
Yes, I would have to say that a new Liberal government alone cannot solve all of our economic problems. There is no single magical solution. However I believe that a new Liberal government will make an important difference, a real difference for the better for all Canadians.
In order to make this economic change, we will have to establish new partnerships with all stakeholders in this country-the private sector, the unions, the provinces, the municipalities, the voluntary agencies-and we will have to stop, once and for all, to pit these groups against one another, as the Tories have been doing for nine years.
In a recent speech the distinguished economist, Judith Maxwell, said:
A society that stops building for tomorrow gets stale and
deteriorates.
That is what has happened to Canada under the last nine years of Conservative rule. Conservatives have stopped investing in order to build for tomorrow. They have stopped investing in people, education, research and development. They have stopped investing in our country's infrastructure. They have stopped investing in the building blocks of a prosperous and competitive economy. As a consequence of the Conservatives not investing in our future, the Canadian economy continues to falter and our high standard of living, perhaps a lot less high since the Conservatives got in, is at risk. The future of our children is at risk.
This Conservative government has failed to respond to the challenges of a new world economy. It has failed to put people back to work. It has failed to offer a real future for our young people. Conservatives simply do not get it. They simply do not realize what has to be done. They have forgotten, or they do not want to agree, as a very wise person said to me this morning, that for Canadians there is a society to be maintained, cultures to be encouraged and a country to be built. Instead of a crusade for a better and more prosperous Canada, the Conservatives have simply presented a budget that is an admission of defeat, a shroud for a dying government.
This is not a budget to respond to the economic and social needs of Canadians. Instead, unfortunately, it is a budget designed to respond to the political needs of the Tory leadership candidates. There is no plan in this budget to get the economy moving quickly forward again

April 27, 1993

and to create more jobs for the 1.5 million unemployed and the young people entering the labour force who are seeking a future and who deserve a future.
However the fact is that the needs of Canada for economic growth and jobs have to come ahead of the ambitions of the Conservative leadership candidates and their misguided expectation that somehow they will be able to perpetuate their years in office. These needs of Canada for economic growth and jobs must come first. However that will happen only once we have an election in which this tired Conservative government, even with a new leader, will be replaced by a new Liberal government, a Liberal government with a strong economic action plan and with the mandate to implement it.
I conclude by moving:

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday's budget is clearly the budget of a tired government. In fact it is the budget of a bankrupt government that is leaving a country bankrupt.
It is incredible that we have a government that is leaving very shortly, and hopefully as quickly as possible when we have the next election, and is leaving this country in a situation in which there is the highest
The Budget
number of unemployed Canadians we have ever had, the highest debt and the highest number of bankruptcies. Nothing in this budget addressed any of those issues. Nothing in this budget gave hope to Canadians. A government without vision leaves a country without hope, and that is the legacy of almost nine years of Tory leadership.
The crisis we have in this country now is a fiscal crisis. There are those who say that the only way we can deal with the fiscal crisis is to create a human crisis. That is what this government has done. The human deficit of unemployment is incredible in this country. While the official statistics rest at 11 per cent, there are many studies that indicate one in four Canadians are either unemployed or underemployed and are seeking employment in this country, or better employment.
It is unbelievable that this government could stand up yesterday and present a budget to this House that was based on continuing unemployment of 11 per cent this year and further double digit unemployment in the next year. It seems that level of unemployment is acceptable to this government. One million children living in poverty is acceptable to this government, if we look at this budget. Hundreds of thousands of people using food banks is acceptable to this government.
Three years ago this House stood together and said that we would eradicate poverty by the year 2000 and this government chose to bring in its last budget which did not even acknowledge the level of poverty it has created in this country. It is a shame.
The government did have choices. Did it choose to do anything about jobs? No it did not. It chose to ignore the example of many of our trading partners, the United States, Japan and Europe, which have very recently introduced jobs plans, of investing in growth and developing a dynamic and modem economy to take us into the 21st century.
Why did this government choose to ignore the fact that our economy is simply not working? To the contrary, it continued with more of the same and said that the cure for the devastation it has created is more devastation. We on this side of the House, the New Democratic Party, say Canadians will not accept that, Canadians will not let the Tories get away with that.
There is one major reason that the Canadian economy is not working and it is that Canadians are not working.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
A recovery without jobs is no recovery at all. A future without jobs is a future without hope. That is unacceptable. It is a betrayal of the people this government is here to serve.
Is the government attacking the deficit? No. With a deficit of $35 billion this year and a deficit of almost $33 billion next year, this exercise is a failure. And why did the government fail? Because it has refused to stop wasting money and because it will not admit that the best way to reduce the deficit is to attack unemployment. The government could have cancelled the helicopter purchase, a deal that will cost the government nearly $6 billion for helicopters to be used to fight an enemy who, since the end of the cold war, no longer exists.
No, it chose to reduce unemployment insurance benefits, to reduce federal regional development grants and transportation subsidies for farmers. It preferred to reduce subsidies for institutions like the CBC, those institutions that unite and define us as a country.

The government had the opportunity to close tax loopholes to the powerful and wealthy and end the private family trust exemption that cost up to $600 million each year. It had the opportunity to cancel the business entertainment deduction that costs up to $1 billion each year.
It chose instead to make life more difficult for low income Canadians by reducing the number of times the GST rebate is received to twice a year from four times a year. I know that people who have jobs and those on the government side who are living quite comfortably may not understand the real life that many low income Canadians live. They may not understand that change will really cause a severe hardship to many families.
In addition, the government chose to cut development assistance to the world's poorest citizens and made drastic cuts to advocacy groups that generally speaking, on very limited budgets, give a voice to those who are less powerful in our society.
Let us look at what the government did in this budget. It made sure that any cuts made were to those with the
least power and the least voice. Those who were exempted from any sacrifice were those with the most: the rich, the powerful and those with private family trusts. Those revenues would have offset any savings by far.
This is a political budget and not a financial budget. The government made the political choice to really get the unemployed and the victims who feel powerless but it is not going to touch its friends who fund its party and will fund the next election. No, no, it is going to leave them alone.
Canadians know and want a government that stands on the side of all Canadians and not just one segment of Canadians. Mr. Speaker, as the leader of the New Democratic Party I say to you there is only one party that stands on the side of all Canadians and that is the New Democrats.
The reality is that the poorest fifth of Canadians own one-third of one per cent of the wealth in this country. The richest fifth of Canadians own 69 per cent of the wealth of this country. Have those in the richest one-fifth been asked to contribute, to sacrifice? No, they have not. Have they been asked to pay their fair share? Not at all.
Why not? As I said earlier it is because this government serves its friends. That is probably one of the saddest things for Canadians about this budget. Canadians did not understand it before but it is clear this government acts as a voice for private greed and not as a voice for public interest and the common good.
It is long past the time we had a government that could recapture that spirit of the public interest and common good in this country so all Canadians can benefit from the riches of our country.
Recently-I was flying back from my riding-I was sitting in the airport beside a couple of people who were discussing what they had been doing. They said they had taken their families to Europe skiing and were intending to travel a bit in Europe. They were looking forward to what they were going to do in the summer. At the end of that conversation they said they were very concerned that governments are not really cutting back social spending and health care.
April 27, 1993

The day before that I was sitting in a union hall in Faro, Yukon, in my riding where hundreds of workers are laid off and others are in danger of losing their positions. We sat and talked about the devastation to their families; the fact that labour laws did not protect them; the fact that these workers were last call on anything that might happen in terms of receiving their benefits and what was owed to them. They could not understand why a government would not protect the working people of this country.
The contrast between those two incidents is graphic. Once again I say that those who have the most are asked to pay the least. The working people who compose the engine that drives this country are asked to make the most sacrifices and are last in line when this government makes its policy and when it draws up a budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame, shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Unemployment is at 11 per cent and it is killing the Canadian economy. It is killing our productivity, our ability to grow and the hopes of many Canadians whether they are miners in Faro, auto workers in Ontario or fish plant workers in the Atlantic.
The OECD has determined that Canada has the largest gap between actual output and potential output of any major industrialized nation in modem history. That output gap translates into lost production of goods and services of more than $70 billion.
As I mentioned earlier, the other gap we have is between those who have the most and those who have the least. We are now spending $80 billion a year to provide services for those who are unemployed and in poverty. Let us attack that deficit. Let us attack the real deficit, the human deficit and also the financial deficit created by unacceptable unemployment rates. To not do so is insulting to those Canadians who are truly suffering across this country.
This morning I met with a group of farmers who really do not know what their future is going to be, yet surely there is nothing more basic than the sovereignty of food. The agricultural industry is both an important part of our economy and an important part of our own well-being. Yet they feel abandoned by this government and by Canadians. Surely this is the group we should be most
The Budget
concerned about in terms of our national well-being as well as our economic well-being.
Would it not be a change if we had a government that chose to act like a government, accepted responsibility for the people within its borders, stopped simply depending and hoping in some Disney-like fashion that if the economies of Europe, Japan and the United States improve then Canada will somehow be dragged along?
We are better than that. We have some of the most skilled workers. We have a strong agricultural community. We have men and women who are building this country into what they hope it can be. The government obviously does not have the least bit of faith in Canadians because its plan is to see if somehow Canada can get dragged along on the hopes of other countries.
Is it not time Canadians and the Canadian government stood up with pride and said they had ideas, initiative and spirit? We live in a country that looks outward to other countries but we stand proud and free. We can succeed because we have the people to do it.
We will never bring down the deficit and the debt unless we get Canadians back to work. We do not have to be economists to figure out that decreasing revenues are a direct result of fewer people working. The deficit is a symptom.
Let us take a moment to look at how the deficit was created. The government brought in a high interest rate policy, a high dollar policy, a bad trade deal and the GST all at the same time. It really led us down the path. It says it is a recession but it is not. It is a made-in-Canada depression and those one in four Canadians who are looking for jobs or looking for better jobs do not just see this as some vague kind of jobless recovery. They look to those in the government to stand up for them and say: "We care about you, we have a jobs plan to address this, we are going to do it, we have the courage, we have the guts and we are going to put it before Parliament," but not this government.
What about the projections of the government? Last year it missed its budget projection on the deficit reduction by about $8 billion and clearly again it was because of a shortfall in tax revenues.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
We need a government that will stand up and say it is not going to attack the unemployed, it is going to attack unemployment. It is about time.

I think we should remind the government of the following important equation: more people on the labour market means more tax revenue. More people on the labour market means that fewer Canadians will depend on the government to get by. Increased revenue combined with a drop in income support payments like unemployment insurance will reduce the deficit. The government has failed to understand this equation. And Canadians are paying the price. It is about time the government paid the price for its own incompetence, and that time will come on election day.

The government predicts a much rosier picture in terms of deficit reduction and unemployment four or five years down the road. The only good news is that it will not be there four or five years down the road.
This is the last budget of this Conservative government. Otherwise I would suggest it call in someone from The National Enquirer to develop its projections because it has about the same legitimacy. Sometimes The National Enquirer is actually much more accurate with its yearly predictions than the finance minister.
How do we get the economy moving and create jobs for Canadians? The Liberals have not offered any answers. The Reform Party's solution is to totally destroy the social foundation on which our economy is based.
We need a jobs plan in this country and only the New Democratic Party has presented a plan that will create 1.6 million new jobs over the next five years. According to independent analysis, it would bring down inflation and the deficit. It would not tax lower and middle-income Canadians further.
The government is right when it says ordinary Canadians cannot afford to pay any more taxes. We agree. After all it is this government that increased taxes on the average family by over $1,900 a year. It has devastated our economy with the GST and it is only fitting for the thief to recognize there is nothing more to steal.

The New Democratic Party has an economic strategy based on full employment, which will put the economy back on track. We have formulated the following specific proposals: a national infrastructure reinforcement program; a national daycare program; a national investment fund; investment in research and development; development of new technology; and fiscal and monetary policies that set a priority on job creation.
Our plan would end bad trade deals that have cost Canadians thousands and hundreds of thousands of jobs. It would introduce a fair tax system where the rich and large corporations finally pay their fair share.
This is a tired government. We understand. We are tired of the government too. It is a bankrupt government. It is a government without vision. Its way is not working. That is the bottom line. Its way does not work and we do not need more of its way which does not work for Canadians.
Unemployment at these levels cannot be sustained. It is a human waste. It is an economic waste and it is a national shame. The source of that shame, the Conservative government, must be defeated.
This country is capable of great things but we cannot in the budget presented by the Minister of Finance see anything great. There is more to this country and there is more hope for Canadians than this government has offered.
This government in nine years has destroyed this country. We in the New Democratic Party say, call that election. You will get the message from Canadians and New Democrats will help to build a new, better and more prosperous Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to the remarks of the Leader of the New Democratic Party.
Part of her remarks I actually agreed with in total. The concern that I have has to do with small business. We all know the greatest hope for new job creation lies with the small business sector in this country.

We have home based businesses, small businesses where people might employ only three, four or five people. There are close to 1.3 million such businesses in Canada. They are finding it very difficult to get access to capital.
The financial institutions in this country are just not playing ball. The government made a commitment to all of us in this House a few months ago that the Small Businesses Loans Act would be the financial instrument to put capital back into the hands of the small business sector.
The government made a commitment that it would promote that bill. It has not lived up to it. This sector to me is our greatest hope. I did not really get a sense, and I say this respectfully, from her remarks that that sector was getting support. I would like her to deal with that.
I would like to know what the New Democratic Party would do to try to make the banks wake up and realize that in addition to finding money for the Reichmanns, the Bronfmans, the Campeaus and a lot of other developers in this country, they should take the time to go out and make small business loans which are the source of this new job hope.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member raises a very important question. As he well knows, being very familiar with this, small business creates about 80 per cent of the new jobs in our economy. Therefore there must be a lot of attention paid to this.
The member is quite right. It has certainly been my experience across Canada that access to capital for small business for new initiatives and in some cases for continuing initiatives is very limited.
In a lot of areas but particularly in rural areas, in areas outside central Canada, it is often more difficult. That is why seeing the government reducing regional development funding is incredible. Some of that regional development funding of course would go directly to small business.
It is also quite incredible in this time of depression and recession when one sees that one of the major banks in Canada over the last two years made $1 billion profit.
It would seem to me that a government interested in small business would bring bank presidents together, would begin to talk about this and would begin to
The Budget
implement policies that would under the Bank Act make loans to small business, obviously ones that were accountable and feasible, as a real part of banks' responsibilities to this country.
I would say also that in the New Democratic Party's jobs plan we propose a national investment fund. The idea of that fund is specifically directed to the member's point about encouraging small business, in making sure that private funds, public funds and regional funds directed by regional boards are directed to investment in just exactly those kinds of enterprises that are appropriate to each region of the country. I think we have seen that a highly centralized system of encouraging regional development often does not work because the people of that area who obviously know the most about that area both in economic terms and in a business sense have not been the ones that have been able to make those decisions.
There are also many changes that can be made to reduce the paper burden on small businesses. I am sure anyone in this House who has either been in small business as I have or others will know that the GST has phenomenally increased the administrative burden, pa-raticularly for smaller businesses.
That is why we in this party propose to eliminate the GST over a period of time. We feel this would put more money in the hands of consumers. It would reduce and make the business climate more favourable specifically for small business and it would create jobs as has already been indicated by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.
I am certainly in agreement with the member that small business must be the real focus of any plan for the economy. I look forward to seeing the Liberals' plan for small business when they have a plan.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak today in support of the budget that my colleague, the Minister of Finance, presented yesterday.
It is interesting that the budget comes at the same time as spring. I see a lot of symbolism in that because, as everyone knows, spring in Canada always brings with it a feeling of optimism and dynamism. This budget will give Canadians what they need for new growth, new jobs and renewed prosperity.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
Of course, success never comes without effort. As Corneille wrote in Polyeucte, "Do we have to win so many times before we triumph?" Canada has had to face so many economic and financial challenges in the last several years that it seemed at times as though we would never get there and would always have to start over.
Today we see that these efforts were not in vain. The budget presented by my colleague, the Minister of Finance, clearly shows us that we were right not to doubt and not to give up but to follow his lead he gave us with the unconditional support and unshakable determination of our Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney.
I would like to talk to you today about some measures in the budget which I think are particularly important and of some effects that the budget will have, especially in the department for which I am responsible, the Department of Transport.
The first objective of the 1993 budget is our number one priority: freeing the Canadian economy so that it can grow and create the jobs we need. For that, we must lighten the burden our economy and our people are saddled with as a result of the deficit and the debt.
During his pre-budget consultations, the Minister of Finance found an unprecedented concern over the excessive borrowing and spending habits of federal and provincial governments.
Canadians definitely want less government borrowing, lower taxes, more jobs and greater choices for the future. Canadians saw what happened when governments acted as though they could add to the debt indefinitely. Taxpayers pay more and more to receive less and less service from the government when interest payments take a growing share of every dollar in tax revenue. Higher and higher taxes slow down the economy, and reduce economic activity, decrease growth and employment.
The 1993 budget answers these concerns by considerably tightening the spending restrictions presented in the economic and fiscal statement of last December. In its main proposals, the budget first imposes no new taxes; second, saves over $30 billion in spending reductions and other measures that will be implemented over the next
five years. This means that the government will restrict the growth in program spending; that is, there will be no real growth in spending, not counting interest charges on the public debt. Third, it is reducing the cost of the federal government by streamlining its activities, reducing the regulatory burden and improving efficiency.

The goal of the budget, the Minister of Finance said, is to free the economy for more job creating growth by steadily reducing the burden of deficits and debt. Transportation is not immune from such a balancing exercise. Fiscal restraint must be shared by all Canadians.
However, Canada is a trading nation and transportation will remain a cornerstone of our economic well-being. The government has recognized the importance of transportation infrastructure in guaranteeing our future economic prosperity. Indeed, the diverse nature of Canada's economy places ever-increasing importance on a safe and efficient transportation system that will allow us to meet the growing challenges of the new global economy.
Major new strategic capital investments in Canada's national transportation and communications networks are under way. Agreements have been signed with five provinces to improve hundreds of kilometres of highways and to create many thousands of jobs. An additional
15,000	person-years of employment are expected to be provided from further projects to be announced in the weeks and months ahead.
These transportation improvement initiatives are being funded out of savings from last year's budget and the December economic and fiscal statement. The measures have been implemented and they are working.
I do not need to underscore the importance of the highway network in Canada. Canadians make around 90 per cent of their trips by car and bus. Close to 60 per cent of freight traffic moves by truck. Recent studies have demonstrated that certain sections of the national highway system do not meet the increasing needs of highway transport. This situation creates safety problems and results in congestion and delays for travellers and commerce. Millions of dollars are lost each year when travellers and freight are tied up in traffic jams.
April 27, 1993

The Government of Canada has recognized this and has invested strategically in the construction and maintenance of highway infrastructure which will generate important benefits in terms of improved safety and economic growth.

As for the equipment used by Transport Canada to carry out its mandate, we will examine the possible benefits of privatizing our helicopter fleet. We will also take a thorough look at the fleet and aircraft service activities to determine the most economic way to provide the service. A pilot project will be implemented to use private sector resources for flight inspection services in Western Canada, provided technical accuracy can be assured. International experience has proven that the private sector can provide similar services more efficiently and economically, while maintaining high safety standards.
In the area of subsidies for transportation and agriculture, the grants and contributions provided in the Western Grain Transportation Act, the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act and the Maritime Freight Rates Act will be reduced by 15 per cent in 1995-96 and 20 per cent in each of the following two years. This has already been the subject of several discussions with the appropriate authorities.
Services have been rationalized and VIA Rail's operating budget will be reduced by $50 million in 1995-96 and by $100 million for each of the following two years. Although I expect there will be a strong reaction to this initiative, VIA Rail has already demonstrated a flexibility and determination beyond what had previously been predicted.
Responsible sound management and corporate restructuring have allowed VIA Rail to fulfil its mandate and even to cut its dependence on government funds further than expected while continuing to provide first class rail passenger services across Canada. VIA Rail's restructuring was necessary due to its spiralling financial requirements which led to our decision in 1990 to reduce its funding by half. This in turn led to a 50 per cent reduction in VIA Rail's services.
The Budget
During the three years since the reduction, VIA Rail has been able to improve its performance substantially. It has managed to provide transcontinental corridor and remote services at funding levels below those authorized by the government. As well, its service to the public has improved. Its on-time performance now exceeds 90 per cent and most of its trains are now equipped with LRC equipment or rebuilt cars.
In 1992 VIA Rail was able to increase its train frequencies on the Montreal-Ottawa-Toronto routes without any increase in its need for resources. It will take VIA Rail some time to analyse the impact of the cuts on train services and the corporation's work force and to prepare a strategy for its new commercial mandate. We expect an announcement on the impact on train services in late 1993 or early 1994.

These measures, together with the many others detailed in the budget, will maintain the 1993-94 deficit at the projected level of $32.6 billion and will considerably reduce the federal deficit in the next five years, as the recovery now under way strengthens.
By 1997-98, the government will end all new borrowing, both in Canada and abroad. Interest payments on the debt will decline to 26 cents per dollar of revenue, compared to 36 cents in 1990-91. The deficit will be reduced to $8 billion, less than 1 per cent of national revenue, compared to 5.1 per cent in 1991-92.
With the measures to stimulate the recovery in the budget of February 1992 and the economic statement last December, the Canadian economy has created over
200,000	full-time jobs since last August.
We are now in a good position to gradually improve our economic performance; our real growth will be nearly 3 per cent in 1993 and over 4.5 per cent in 1994, while inflation and interest rates will remain low.
More than ever, Canadians want their governments to co-operate for the sake of economic prosperity and international competitiveness. They want a national solution to the national debt problem and want governments to act without delay. The Minister of Finance has already invited his provincial and territorial counterparts to Ottawa in late May to begin working on this.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
With the 1993 federal budget, the government has a responsible and achievable plan to restore the nation's finances and strengthen our economy's ability to create jobs.

speechtext:

The minister said in his comments that the burden imposed by the deficit and the debt had to be alleviated, thereby implying that the government had managed to do so, when in fact it is the opposite, as we well know.
The government failed miserably on this issue, and I wonder if the minister recognizes the magnitude of this failed attempt.
The minister knows full well that the deficit for the year which just ended last March 31 will be of the order of $35.5 billion. He also knows-if he read today's newspapers-that nobody believes the economic forecasts contained in yesterday's budget. We are told that real growth will reach 4.5 per cent in 1994. The government is dreaming in colour.
During the eighties, there was significant economic growth because of the strength of the American economy and the strength of growth and consumption in Canada. However, I want to emphasize that nobody believes that the recovery in the United States will be as strong this time as it was in the eighties, and I also want to refer to one of the indicators mentioned on page 42 of yesterday's budget. For the current year, the government anticipates an increase of only 0.5 per cent in the personal income of Canadians, while the population will grow by about 1.5 per cent. This means that Canadians will suffer a net loss of income. Instead of having-

Mr. Speaker, I think that my hon. colleague, like all hon. members of this House, will recognize that no one in the world has infallible means
of predicting what is going to happen in the years ahead. Everybody has their own prediction tools and it is always on that basis that all calculations are made.
I think that we are in very good company when we base our forecasts on those of such a reputable and absolutely impartial organization as the International Monetary Fund, which has been saying for months now that in 1993-94, Canada will have the highest growth rate in the world. We are basing our predictions and forecasts on such in-depth and reliable analyses as those of the International Monetary Fund.
The people of Canada must be absolutely delighted with what the Conservative government has achieved over the past nine years and what it is planning for the future, as compared to the statement the leader of the Liberal Party made in his riding of Shawinigan just last Sunday that, if elected, his party would try to bring the deficit down only to 3 per cent of Gross Domestic Product, while the measures we are putting into place at this time will reduce the deficit much more.
What is even more disturbing and disquieting for the population as a whole to realize is that not only did his party put this country thoughtlessly in debt the last time it was in power, but he is now proposing to maintain the deficit indefinitely at $25 billion a year. If ever there was one thing that should alert Canadians to the dangers that lie ahead if that party were to come back to power, it is this very statement by the leader of the Liberal Party.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport regarding the cuts to VIA Rail and also to the CBC.
Back in 1981 when Jean-Luc Pepin was Minister of Transport he decided to cut VIA services by 19 per cent. At that time the now Minister of Finance led a Conservative Party task force across the country to find out the views of Canadians on the appropriateness of VTA Rail passenger services. The report he issued on behalf of his colleagues said in part: "The task force affirms that the federal government has a responsibility to ensure that rail services in Canada be retained, modernized and expanded as an important part of our national transportation system."
April 27, 1993

We know and the minister in his own comments reminded us of the 50 per cent cut in the subsidy level to VIA a little over two years ago. He pointed out that there will be further cuts. In fact, by the year 1997-98 the VIA subsidy will be $138 million.
The question I want to put to the Minister of Transport is, how can he expect VTA Rail to continue to operate outside of the Windsor-Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal-Quebec City corridor if that is the level of subsidy that is going to be available?
As he knows, the routes from Toronto to Vancouver, and the routes from Montreal to the Atlantic do not and never can pay their own way. Why has he and his government decided to put an end to VTA Rail? That is really what it amounts to. Why is he not prepared to invest in the national unity of this country to ensure that people can travel to see each other, to meet each other and to visit this great country? Why is the government doing that when it should be funding it properly and providing new capital services?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I certainly agree with the point of order raised by the hon. member I would simply point out that indeed portable telephones might well improve the quality of answers coming from the minister.

It just proves that the government has completely lost contact with reality. For the second time in four months, the Minister of Finance intended to propose a supposedly growth oriented budget plan. Mr. Speaker, as you can see from yesterday's budget, the only thing that could be growing is the frustration of the Canadian people toward a government that refuses to take the necessary steps to give them hope once again.

This has not been a simple recession. We have gone through a fundamental restructuring of the world's economy, a restructuring that has been made worse in this country as a result of the monetary and fiscal policies followed by this government.
The problem is that we are not alone in this restructuring and it is the failure of this government to understand this simple fact that has led to its projections consistently not being met; $1 billion out in the deficit in the last four months, $8 billion out in the deficit in the last year, projections which have made this government the laughing stock of governments around the world.
We can live with that I suppose because its life is so short lived. Those who cannot live with this government's failures are the 1.6 million unemployed in this country, those who are on welfare, the ever-increasing army of the working poor. The Minister of Finance stands up here and talks of double-digit employment as if it is a simple statistic on a written page.
I would ask them to leave the written page and go into the real world. Come into my riding and see what it is like when families are broken up, see what it is like when young people are condemned to a decade of no jobs and suddenly begin to realize that the life for which they had such hope has disappeared before them.
There are four keys to job creation. The first is a lowering of our real interest rates, putting this country on a competitive basis with the rest of the world. In yesterday's budget the interest rates projected by this government continue for the next five years at historically high levels, far higher than our competitors, far higher than will make it possible for us to develop a competitive economy.
When one looks at the reactions of the world's financial community to this budget one must be fearful that interest rates will continue to rise and under those circumstances we will be plunged once again into recession. We will be plunged once again into a period of deflation while the rest of the world continues its restructuring and young Canadians begin to ask themselves if indeed there is a future for them in this country.
The second key is retraining. Nothing in this budget recognizes that the most important natural resources in this country do not lie buried deep in the ground. They lie in the skills and talents of those who walk upon it.
Research and development is the third key. This budget deals with research and development as tokenism. It talks of mechanisms, it talks of exploring, it talks of process but there is nothing concrete to enable Canadians to build an innovative economy. There is nothing in this budget that will allow us to take on both the Germans and the Japanese, those who are meeting the modern challenges.
There is no mention of environmental technologies, medical technologies and the great growth areas which are required if we are going to create the jobs of tomorrow.
Finally the fourth key is small and medium sized business. My colleague from Broadview-Greenwood has been so articulate in this House on the subject. What does the budget say about small business, that area of the economy which is creating 85 per cent of all the jobs in this country? It is virtually silent. Is it because small and medium sized businesses are Canadian-owned and that this government looks south for its economic direction and not within the heart and fabric of the Canadian nation?
The multinationals of tomorrow are today being created by two people in back sheds. This is happening right around the world and it is not happening in
April 27, 1993

Canada. That is why Canadians are losing faith. It is why they have lost faith with this government.
When the Liberals take power within the next three months-maybe four months depending upon when this government finally summons the courage to go to the Canadian people-we will once again give Canadians the tools and the confidence to rise to the challenges that lie outside our borders.

What is most astonishing in this budget is that, while Canadian taxpayers seem willing to directly address the deficit, the Minister of Finance instead served them a rehash, in a context so optimistic as to make everyone dream.

The 1993-94 budget is the last Tory budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank God.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank heaven.
It is also the last budget to be written according to the conventional wisdom of old style politics. The hallmarks of political budget-making are stamped on every page of this very lean document; dubious deficit forecasts, inflated economic assumptions.
This budget demonstrates the government's fiscal, economic and intellectual bankruptcy. For better or for worse the people of Canada are adjusting to very different economic circumstances. Every business, every volunteer group, every association in the country is coping with change. It is very clear-if there was any doubt of it before-after yesterday's budget that this government is not.
In the real world off Parliament Hill and outside the dynamics of the Tory leadership race that this budget was designed to comfort, a political revolution is under way. Canadians are demanding an end to the volleys of taxation that issue from the nation's capital every spring. They are demanding that governments cease their political fiddling while our prosperity burns.
In a thousand ways the central issue of our time, the reordering of the relationships between Canadians and their governments, is intruding on the business as usual world of politics and government; the rejection of executive federalism.
The Budget
The popular uprising against a British Columbia proposed homeowners' tax in March of this year and the massive unpopularity of governments from coast to coast all bespeak a deep and an urgent hunger for change. Canadians are demanding nothing less than an end to the political economy of governments that can neither follow the wishes of their citizens today nor bring before them the questions that must be decided tomorrow.
The challenge facing Canada is twofold. An immediate reordering of our public finances must be undertaken to avert a fiscal crisis. At the same time a reordering of the politics that underlie our financial problems must occur. The failure to meet either challenge will result in the failure to meet both.
Liberals propose to confront this challenge head on. Canadians must take full possession of the reordering of their public finances. There must be a new covenant between Canadians and the three senior levels of government. Growth strategies and mechanisms for their achievement must be arrived at. Plans for improving the cost efficiency of government services through a deep restructuring must be adopted. The tax structure must be reordered.
Again, my colleague from Broadview has been so articulate as indeed my colleague from London, those who really have brought forth a new vision as to how Canadians can govern themselves, can tax themselves and can bring themselves out of the depths of despair into which this government has unfortunately plunged them. A fundamental evaluation of the respective roles, the responsibilities and the powers of taxation of all three levels of government must be undertaken.
In the debates that take place between governments, why is it that the federal and provincial governments can seemingly continue to ignore municipal governments, those who are on the front line of social change? Why is it that they ignore the business community, the volunteer associations and the sole taxpayer who is at the bottom of this incredible pyramid of cost and efficiency led by this Conservative government?
Irregular taxation among jurisdictions has produced economic distortions, inefficient and wasteful collection costs and a perverse sense that the tax system is irrational and unfair.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
Canadians are prepared to pay their fair share of taxes. What they object to is when they see discrimination against them in favour of others. What they object to is when they see that the services that they have come to expect cut back and their taxes going up. There is a deep feeling that the system is warped against Canadians. Over the last nine years in fact that is the legacy of this government.
We will not solve the debt problem in this country without a national consensus on what it is reasonable to ask of the Canadian taxpayer and unless there is a consensus on how he or she is to be taxed.
We have a phenomenal opportunity to build one of the great countries of the world. The problems of this nation are not going to be solved by jargon and rhetoric. They are going to be solved by a nation which is able to achieve great things together.
The budget speaks to the government's economic plan. The budget sets out to the Canadian people the plan by which it sees them achieving this greatness, by which it sees them competing with other countries in the world whose economies are prospering. If that is the case and this budget is the best this government can do, what hope is there for Canadians?
Yesterday we were in the lock-up for four hours. I expected to be occupied. I read the document in 20 minutes. The government explained it to us in five minutes. In fact it did not even send in the departmental officials until the very end because there was not enough to explain.
Why did we have this budget? It was a non-event. Why did we have the last December statement? It was a non-event. Has this government run out of ideas and imagination?

My God, we could do a better budget on this side in the next five minutes than that government has done in the last four months.

This budget is nothing more than the last wishes of a government that has decided to throw in the towel. This government has been promising us for almost nine years now that it would firmly attack the deficit. It has failed totally. The federal government and the provinces are now deeper in debt than ever before. And the saddest thing in all of that is that this budget will never be successful in reassuring international financial markets, which was one of the goals of this exercise.
Because he wanted to leave all options open to the next leader of the government, the Minister of Finance is jeopardizing the economic health of the whole country. Canadians have had enough of this mascarade. Young people on social welfare and the unemployed have had enough of this mascarade. We are wasting valuable time. The citizens of this country have the right to judge now. The curtain must fall on this government, and the sooner the better.

The time has come to let the Canadian people judge if what they want is the empty vessel served up by this government or a political party, a movement and a consensus which understands that we will solve the deficit through growth, that we will give Canadians hope through growth, that we will resolve the national unity problem by giving Canadians from coast to coast, from British Columbia to Newfoundland, a goal to believe in. That is the Liberal vision.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this government was elected to office almost nine years ago the biggest challenge facing us was to restore some fiscal sanity to our economy. Now nine years later, where are we? Some will complain that the deficit is almost as high today as it was in September 1984. Others will criticize us because the national debt has more than doubled since we took office. It would be instructive to review the past
April 27, 1993

nine years and seriously look at these comments in the light of economic realities today.
In 1984 this government inherited a national debt of $206 billion. When the Liberals were elected in 1968 the debt stood at only $18.8 billion but when they left it was $206 billion. During that 17-year period Canada's debt increased and became 11 times higher. By comparison, since 1984 the debt has grown from the inherited $206 billion to $458 billion for this year.
On the surface it would seem reasonable for the opposition Liberal Party to complain that the debt has doubled under Conservative management. However the comparison soon wears thin when one considers that rather than 11 times higher, which happened while the Liberals were in office, it is now over twice as high. On top of that, this government has not added one cent to the debt since 1987.
From 1970 to 1984 a surplus of $220 million became a deficit of $38.5 billion under the Liberal administration. Government spending was out of control. Those are not just my words but those are the words of the Auditor General who in the mid-1970s said he was deeply concerned "that Parliament, indeed the government, had lost or was close to losing effective control of the public purse." He then went on to say: "Federal management and control in the Government of Canada is grossly inadequate." That is what the Auditor General said while the Liberals were in office.
During the Trudeau years, government spending on programs had increased at an average annual rate of 13.8 per cent, far in excess of inflation. If this trend had been allowed to continue after 1984 the result would have been catastrophic. If we had allowed spending to continue at the same average pace as the Liberals, the national debt would have sky-rocketed from $206 billion when we inherited it to over $900 billion today, rather than the $458 billion. This year's annual deficit would be over $85 billion rather than the $32.6 billion for this fiscal year.
We could not leave this burden to our children and to our grandchildren. Action was needed and action was taken. Barely two months into our first term, the Minister of Finance laid out our economic plan, a plan that has been adhered to in every single budget including this one, nine budgets and five economic statements in a row.
The Budget
What have we done? Every single budget and every economic statement that this government has offered to Canadians has cut spending. Every single one and every time the opposition complained about our cutting of spending.
Since 1985 a total of $118 billion has been cut by this government. Added to that the December economic statement cut spending by $8 billion. This budget further cuts spending this year by $3.8 billion and next year by $5.8 billion, totalling $30.7 billion over the next five years.
Compared to the average annual increase of 13.8 per cent of the Liberal 15-year period, our program spending since 1985 has averaged only 3.9 per cent per year. Beginning in 1991 the Spending Control Act was passed by Parliament that legislated an annual ceiling of 3 per cent per year. With the measures of this budget, the average program spending will now be held at only 1.5 per cent over each of the next five years. This is well below inflation. The 1.5 per cent average annual increase will be the lowest we have seen in Canada since the early 1950s, or 40 years ago.
The contrast is even more dramatic when compared to the 9.3 per cent under the current Liberal leader when he was Minister of Finance. More astonishing were the increases the present Liberal leader permitted when he was President of the Treasury Board: 16.3 per cent in 1976 and 14.6 per cent in 1977. Clearly this contrast shows this government's fiscal responsibility where our actions speak louder than words. No wonder then that the Auditor General just after two years of Conservative management said: "Members of Parliament and the taxpayers of Canada should be heartened by genuine improvements."
It would be instructive to look at the spending habits of provincial governments over the same period of time. While the federal government was spending at an annual average rate of 3.9 per cent from 1984 to 1992, Ontario during the same years spent at a rate of 10.6 per cent and the province was not alone.
For the city of Kitchener in my riding the average annual increase over those same years was 7.5 per cent. The local public school-board's increase was 9.5 per cent. I must mention that the city and the school-board sometimes had to start new programs demanded by the

April 27, 1993
The Budget
province without sufficient funding. Impressive and deep cuts have been made in this year's budget.
It also seems that Premier Rae and his socialist cohorts at Queen's Park are beginning to see the light. No one should be misled by the socialists here or at Queen's Park in Toronto who say that we have just simply passed on our problem to them. Yes, we have asked them to share part of the national problem. However Ontario's own treasury papers tell us that we did not cut our transfer payments to Ontario. Transfers to Ontario, according to its papers, actually increased from 12.9 per cent to 17.2 per cent of total provincial revenues. Remember that these are not my figures; they come straight from the Government of Ontario.
Added to that the impact of our measures on Ontario represented under 1 per cent in the first year and under 2 per cent in subsequent years of the total provincial revenues. All the while Ontario continued spending at an average annual rate of 10.6 per cent while we here in Ottawa over those same years were spending at an average rate of 3.9 per cent.
As I said earlier the national debt has more than doubled since 1984. Also we have not added one penny to the debt since 1987. What does that mean? Quite simply since 1987 we have been running an operating surplus.
In 1985 we ran a $16.1 billion operating deficit in our first year. In effect on top of the annual interest payments on the debt, another $16.1 billion was added to the debt. By 1987 we turned this around. Since then the cumulative effect of the surpluses in each year has actually reduced the national debt by $25 billion.
Since 1984 the government has privatized or dissolved 39 Crown enterprises and other holdings and has improved the operations for the remainder. The number of full-time Crown corporation employees has been reduced by nearly 90,000 individuals.
In 1984 the inflation rate stood at 4.4 per cent. Today it is under 2.5 per cent. Interest rates have fallen from 13 per cent in 1984 to 6 per cent today. Therefore mortgage rates have also tumbled. The annual cost of carrying a five-year $75,000 mortgage has been cut by $3,300 per year since we were first elected.
Even the unemployment rate is lower today at 11 per cent compared to 11.2 per cent in 1984. That is after coming out of the worst economic downturn since the Great Depression of the 1930s.
Job creation features in the 1992 budget and the December statement are now beginning to work and we can see the evidence of that. There are 200,000 new full-time jobs since August of last year and 48,000 new jobs in March of this year. Between 1984 and 1990 more jobs were created in Canada than in all of the following countries combined: France, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Greece, Ireland, New Zealand, Belgium, Switzerland, and Finland. They represent more than four times the population of Canada.
Since 1984 Canada has led all G-7 countries in percentage increase in job creation. According to the OECD, Canada will have the strongest percentage increase in jobs of any major industrialized nation this year and next.
This budget announces a further 10 per cent cut added to the 10 per cent cut in the December 1992 statement. This is to be followed by subsequent cuts of 15 per cent and a cut of 20 per cent for all advocacy groups.
I personally think they should all be at zero. In other words they should all be cut 100 per cent and not this piece-meal of 10, 10, 15 and 20 on top of the cuts we made previously. These advocacy groups should raise all of their money through their own membership and the Government of Canada should give them not one penny.
As it is now we discriminate in favour of liberal leftist feminist groups such as the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and we discriminate against other women's groups such as the conservative-minded group REAL Women. The truth is that all of these advocacy groups, whether right or left, should be cut 100 per cent.
Funding for multicultural groups should also be cut 100 per cent. They should do what other successful ethnic groups, such as the five German clubs in the Kitchener-Waterloo region have successfully done over the years, that is, raise their own money. Those five clubs have never asked for nor received a penny of federal government money and all of them are very successful and are growing.
April 27, 1993

We could then take the money saved and use some of it to enhance Canadian citizenship and pride in being a Canadian. That is exactly why all the immigrants come to Canada in the first place: to be Canadian citizens and to be a part of and live in and contribute to what is the best country in the world in which to live according to the United Nations.
Also, we could take some of this money saved and use it for a package to stimulate the building of new homes. I recommended such cuts and such a stimulative measure to the minister. I recommended a modest mortgage interest deductibility program limited to all first-time buyers of new homes for a 10-year period.
It would help young families to buy new homes. It would stimulate the construction industry. It would put unemployed manufacturing workers back to work rather than drawing on UI benefits and welfare. It would put them to work in housing construction and trades that could be quickly learned. Yes, it would cost money at first. Then in less than two years it would begin to pay it all back and all Canadians would reap the benefits.
Nevertheless I am very pleased to read the following from the budget:
In response to representations on the equity capital needs of smaller, knowledge-based firms, we will also explore ways to develop mechanisms to encourage investors to support local companies and at the same time lend their expertise to help the companies succeed.
This part of the budget is in direct response to an idea developed in the Kitchener-Waterloo, Cambridge and Guelph area under the leadership of Mr. Larry Zepf which I and other area MPs had brought to the Minister of Finance. This must be added to other representations by the MPs from Kitchener-Waterloo, Cambridge and Guelph such as the welcome news of the faster writeoffs of new high-tech equipment in this budget and the additional $230 million for Canadian companies undertaking research and development in the December statement. All will help job creation in our region and across Canada.
In conclusion, the best part of this budget and of the actions taken since 1984 is that because of a disciplined cutting of spending in every budget and after the worst recession since the Depression of the 1930s there is now
The Budget
finally some light at the end of the tunnel. We can now project, if we stay the course and only if we stay the course, the elimination of the annual deficit and we can begin to pay off on our national debt in four years' time.
We can do this without any new taxes. In fact, new taxes will deny consumers the ability to spend and to speed the recovery. If we did cut taxes the socialists in Toronto would just take away for themselves any tax cut we might make, as they did in 1992.
There are only two ways to reduce the deficit: higher revenues and lower spending. The right way to reduce the deficit is to cut spending. The right way to get higher revenues is to encourage economic growth. We cannot do that by raising taxes.
According to international think-tanks, investment agencies and the United Nations, if Canada continues the disciplined course it has been on since 1984 it is poised to lead the world in economic growth over the next few years. We have the opportunity, again if we stay the course and only if we stay the course to eliminate our deficit and to begin to pay down on our debt.
