Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate. Let me say that I was quite surprised by some of the comments made by the member for Kitchener. Even though he sits on that side, he is known to many of us in this Eiouse as generally having some degree of common sense.
I am certain that the people of Kitchener would be quite surprised to hear the member, albeit in a difficult situation, less than 24 hours after a so-called budget that preached the virtues of restraint and everybody doing their fair share, defending as appropriate, wrapping in the flag of patriotism, issuing a call to arms, the Prime Minister's first class, paid, goodbye holiday trip around the world, through Europe and the United States at a cost of millions of dollars. He says it is an appropriate gesture and all Canadians ought to stand, face the flag, salute and feel their heart bursting with pride as the Prime Minister really shows how Canada can spend lavishly at a time of restraint.
I say to the member with great respect that I suspect the people of Kitchener will not appreciate the member for Kitchener taking that view in this regard.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hard working people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me say to the member as well that I hope the people of Kitchener are watching today. If some are watching, I hope they will call up the Kitchener-Waterloo Record, the newspaper in Kitchener and ask it to request a copy of the member's comments.
I do not think they will be impressed with the member's comments at a time of restraint when governments all across the country are putting cuts in place. We are within days of an historical vote in the Soviet Union where the people showed they were committed to democracy. They said yes to Yeltsin, yes to reform, yes to staying the course and not going back to the old ways of the old communist government and the cold war. A massive number, 70 per cent, surprised the planet and said yes to staying the course, yet this government would bring in a budget and keep in place a $6 billion expenditure for cold war helicopters.
Only a few weeks ago the minister of defence was saying: "But we have to keep this expense in place
The Budget
because we do not know what is going to happen in the Soviet Union. Yeltsin may be pushed out. The people may go back to a communist regime."
I do not think anybody on the planet was prepared. A scant few days ago the results came in with a margin of greater than 70 per cent. The hard-pressed people of the Soviet Union, living in difficult circumstances, making great sacrifices and doing without nevertheless embraced democracy by an overwhelming margin in North American terms, an unheard of margin. They wrapped their arms around the concept of democracy and reform and said they would stay the course.
What is Canada's answer to that historic vote? Our answer is to bring in a budget in which we keep in place a $6 billion cold war expenditure. What is the member's comment opposite? It is an appropriate expenditure. We need to spend those billions to watch our enemy, the Soviet Union. Even the United States, the arch enemy of the old and gone Soviet empire has chosen to upgrade over 500 helicopters in its helicopter fleet. Two hundred and thirty nine search and rescue style helicopters have been upgraded at a cost of $10 million each. Over 300 Chinooks have been upgraded by the United States but Canada alone in the world is going to spend nearly $6 billion on helicopters we do not need.
The company in question, Westland Augusta is bankrupt. It has been taken over by an Italian crown corporation. The president of the company has been arrested and charged in a bribery scandal and is now before the courts in Europe. The helicopter in question crashed, killing all the crew and the remaining prototypes have been grounded pending an investigation. Yet this government insists on proceeding-

speechtext:
The hon. member opposite says: "No, no, you cannot say $6 billion, it is only $5.8 billion." Let me tell you about government projections. According to its own budget papers in 1991-92 this government projected a deficit this year of $27.5 billion, which is why it cannot be taken seriously.
Do you know how much it was off by? Can you guess how much it was off by? Was it off by a mere billion? Was it $2 billion?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: More, more, more.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was it $3 billion? Was it $4 billion; $5 billion; $6 billion? Was it $7 billion? Was it $8 billion? It was off by a full $9 billion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was off by $9 billion. This government projected in its last full budget that it would create in the intervening period to this day an additional 500,000 new jobs. How much do you think it was off by? Was it off by 100,000, 300,000, 500,000 or 700,000? It was off by 800,000 because it did not create 500,000 jobs. In the intervening period, the economy has actually lost an additional
300,000	jobs.
How can anybody take the projections of this Minister of Finance and this government seriously?
This budget has been printed on recycled paper and so it should be. It is a recycled document. Only an excellent, first class, used car salesman could call this document a new model this year. This is old, used, abandoned, the tires are flat and the gas tank is empty.
Canadians expected a game plan. They expected the government to invite them to engage in a crusade to rebuild, reinvigorate this country and make it competitive to ensure we can challenge the world and earn our
fair share of this planet's wealth. They were prepared to do their part.
I have just spent weeks in the province of Newfoundland knocking on the doors of some of the poorest people in this country. Do you know what they said? They said governments cannot spend beyond their means. They are not putting their hands out and saying "spend, spend, spend"; they are saying "be responsible." They are saying "be competent"; they are saying "give us a game plan and we will do our part. Invite us to participate in rebuilding this country and restoring confidence. We will do our part."
Then the government yesterday produced this thin, mean, tired, worn out, transparently empty, political patronizing piece of paper called a budget that invites people to just close their eyes to the disaster this government has visited upon this country.
The ship of state of Canada is in the middle of the ocean. The winds are high, the waves are high and she is being battered to and fro. What this ship needs is a steady hand on the wheel. What do we have instead? We have a tired Tory government telling the passengers, the population of Canada, to go back to sleep, that the ship is on course. The course is disaster. This is not just my opinion or the opinion of the members opposite. It is not a journalist's opinion nor the public's opinion. The budget documents tell the story.
What do they say? The Auditor General, as my colleague has made clear, pointed out that in 1984 the public debt of Canada was $157 billion. From the time the country was founded until 1984, 117 years, the total debt acquired in building the infrastructure of the country-the highways, schools, universities, towns, transportation systems-was $157 billion. With that we built and created one of the greatest nations on earth.
What has happened in the intervening nine years? Are there any more highways? Are there any more transportation systems? Have any more great cities been created out of dry land on the Atlantic, on the prairies, in the heartland? No. What has happened to the deficit in the intervening years?
Let us look right in the budget document. All members pick up their documents and turn to page 63. It is right in the document. From the $157 billion it cost to build an entire nation over 117 years, in nine years this
April 27, 1993

government drove the deficit to $458.6 billion at the end of this fiscal year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With over three million people out of work.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And what does it give us for that? What new infrastructure, what new population, what new cities, what new highways, what new hospitals, what new industries?
Mr. Speaker, you have not heard the best part yet. I know your curiosity is now piqued. It is telling us that if we re-elect it four years from now-page 62 of the document-it will add another $100 billion to the national debt. During the life of another government if it is re-elected, the national debt will go up to $563.2 billion, another $105 billion. That is its plan. That is what it is putting on paper. That is what it is admitting to. If everything goes fantastically well it will increase the debt by only another $105 billion.
That is the game plan opposite. This is the party that campaigned on the notion of fiscal responsibility.
Let us look at another page in the budget because I do not want to give you my opinion. You might think it is kind of shaded, given that I would like nothing more than to see this crowd booted out. Let us look at the budget document itself. Let us turn now to page 26. Members of the public who do not have their copy yet should write down the number so they can look at it later when they do have a copy of the budget. On page 26 there is an incredible admission:
Canada's gross international liabilities are partly offset by foreign assets held by Canadians. Nevertheless, relative to the size of the economy, Canada is now by far the most indebted of the major industrial countries. Further, Canada's net foreign liabilities reached a post-war record in 1992 - 43.8 per cent of GDP.
The budget document says that this government has put Canada in the position where we are now the largest debtor nation in the entire industrialized world and that under this government we set a record in 1992. What was the record? We have a post-war record whereby 43.8 per cent of our GDP is our foreign liability. This is our
The Budget
foreign-held debt or Canadian paper held in foreign hands. Of that total, 40 per cent is held by Japan.
I said it was a record. When was the previous record? Let me read on in the document:
Its previous peak was 42 per cent in 1961.
What party was in power in 1961? It was the last time the Tories were in power under Mr. Diefenbaker.
All the rhetoric in the world by the member for Kitchener and by every happy and well-trained member opposite in the Conservative Party will not change the facts contained in their government's own budget document. The legacy of this government is to bring Canada to the point where Canada under this administration in nine years has almost tripled the previous debt piled up in the first 117 years of Confederation and where Canada in the western industrialized world is the largest-bar none and second to none-debtor nation on the planet. One can think of all the countries one wants to.
The Conservatives standing up and saying with that record to the people of Canada: "Re-elect us and we will pile on another $100 billion of debt," is like the pyroma-niac arrested with the match in his hand who says: "Sorry fellows, I was just kidding. I would like now to apply to be fire chief." If it were not so tragic and so serious it would be laughable.
I do not even know why we had a budget yesterday. It was a phoney budget and a phoney exercise. There were no changes in the fiscal arrangements between the federal and provincial governments, no changes in the corporate tax rate, no changes in the personal income tax rate, no initiatives to create jobs or no long-term plans to come to grips with the annual deficit or the long-term debt.
There was only one thing it did that was of any substance and only one way in which it tipped its hand. It did two things. The member for St. John's East cannot be pleased with this. I notice that he is looking distinctly uncomfortable about it. I refer to page 53 in the book. The government indicated that it is not going to renew federal-provincial agreements in the areas of forestry and mining. There will be no more federal-provincial co-operation in forestry or mining. That is important to my area of Corner Brook, Newfoundland, to central Newfoundland, to western Newfoundland and to the forestry sector all across Canada. This sector provides one in every 10 Canadian jobs.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
It wiped out and happily said goodbye to the mining sector. This is also important to my part of the country and to my riding in particular and to the Baie Verte peninsula.
What else was said? It was said that the government will be reviewing the economic and regional development agreements in other sectors as they expire. This includes economic and regional development agreements in agriculture, communications, the environment, fisheries, transportation, industrial development, industrial innovation and tourism. In every area and far-flung region of this country those who have the least among us seek to rebuild their infrastructure, add value to their industrial base and take their natural resource area and build on it to create new wealth. In every area where those who have the least reach out their hands in a sense of co-operation, partnership and building, this federal government is going to withdraw the federal hand and walk away and abandon the regions of Canada. That is the game plan and that statement in the budget makes a mockery of a statement yesterday or two days ago by the Minister of National Defence in Atlantic Canada when she said that she wanted to put more money into regional development. It is an absolute farce.
There is one other important matter. The defence minister said: "If I am elected as leader of the Conservative Party I will wipe out the deficit in five years." The Minister of the Environment said: "If I am elected as leader of the Conservative Party I will wipe out the deficit in four years." That is the claim.
Again, let us look at the budget papers. We want to have an objective opinion. According to the budget papers, the Minister of Finance is forecasting that-even if we believe all of his blown up, hyperventilated, exaggerated claims to growth and productivity which I do not not of course having had experience with believing those things in the past-there will be at least a $14 billion annual deficit on the date by which the Minister of the Environment says we will have no deficit. There will be at least an $8 billion annual deficit on the date by which the Minister of National Defence claims she will wipe out the deficit.
If the leadership candidates for the Conservative Party cannot get their story straight with their own Minister of Finance who is telling us that we cannot wipe out the debt in five years or in four years despite his best efforts, then it is time for Tory leadership candidates to explain precisely to Canadians how they are going to eliminate the debt. Let the Minister of National Defence tell us whether it is old age security, medicare or education funding. What basic programs important to Canadians are going to be wiped out to pay for helicopters and to keep a campaign commitment that was given by someone who had not thought it through?
The ordinary people of Canada, the people who sit in their T-shirts with beers in their hands and with whom the Minister of National Defence cannot relate, know bull when they see it. This budget and these campaign promises both belong in the same category. I cannot say the word in the House, Mr. Speaker. Let me just say this. The people of Canada know a phoney exercise when they see it. It takes a face like a horse's you know what to get up and try to present this budget to the people of Canada as a serious exercise in regulating and managing our economy. This is a shameful and ridiculous exercise that we have engaged in with members opposite.

Before I get into the question and the reference to the pages that he was referring to I would like to talk about that little debate we had on budget figures and why I used $206 billion.
Look at the public accounts for 1991-92 on page 1.2 and table 1.1 that is headed deficit and net debt: "In the year ended March 31, 1984 the net debt was $167.8 billion." I will read further on the same page: "From April 1, 1984 to March 31, 1985 the net debt was $206.3 billion." This is the figure I used.
The reason I used the figure $206.3 billion from the public accounts was that the election was on September 4, 1984. Therefore, I should use the numbers that go after that or are in that current fiscal year. That is the reason I used it.
When I said I stand by the number of $206 billion then I have to use the number of $206 billion because that is the figure in the fiscal year in which we came in. I cannot
April 27, 1993

The Budget
go to the previous year. I have to use the $206 billion. I have no other choice.
I think in the debate we should be careful why we use certain numbers. The member was right to quote $157 billion-I think it was $167 billion-for the previous year. I have no quarrel with that. However, I have to use the number from the fiscal year in which we were elected and that was $206 billion.
I have a few questions. The first question is with regard to page 62.
I have to thank the member, through you Mr. Speaker, for his kind remarks to me. He was very gracious. In trying to be gracious to the member I must say that I enjoy the play acting he does every day in Question Period in the House. I enjoy his choice of words. I think we all do. I think some of us who do not come from Newfoundland envy those from Newfoundland. They have a remarkable ability and use of the English language. We enjoy listening to them and we have just had a good display of that here today. I do not know how much we learned. There was a tremendous amount of heat but I am not sure there was a lot of light.
My question is this. On page 62 he took us through the line of net public debt, which is $458 billion for this year through to $563 billion for 1997-98. That is correct. He was right.
Guess what? I want to ask this question through you, Mr. Speaker. Why did the member ignore the next line? He said nothing about it. That line shows that the financial requirements excluding foreign exchange will go from minus $34.4 billion this year to $1 billion in 1997-98. Why did the member leave that line out?
My second question is this. He quoted page 26 and said: "Look at the damaging things that are said. Canada is now by far the most indebted of the major industrial countries." That is true and exactly right.
Why is it that for nine budgets and five economic statements where we tried to cut spending the member voted against it every single time? Why did he do that? Why did he not join us in cutting the spending? Why did he not support us in cutting the spending?
My last question-

speechtext: Time is running out. In all fairness I have to give the floor to the hon. member.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious to some people that the way to avoid hearing the truth expressed a second time is to make the noise of a stick in an empty barrel and keep pounding away until the clock runs out.
I frankly do not know what the member's great debating point was. If the member stands on his feet and says: "We agree that the deficit or the debt of Canada is going to increase by $105 billion in the next four year if our government is re-elected; there is no argument," then I do not know where he thinks the great debating point in that is.
If he agrees with the budget documents that the annual deficit cannot be wiped out, as is claimed by the two leadership candidates, then I do not know what his argument is.
The member talked about Newfoundlanders having a great-I do not know if it is true or untrue-ability to express themselves but I will say one thing. Where I come from we do not need to try to find semantic arguments in numbers to say things. The people of Canada know when their nation is in trouble.
The people of Canada not just in Newfoundland but all across this country want to do something about it. They want to participate in a plan. We are profoundly disappointed that there is no plan.
What was the great debating point in having the member note that Canada is the largest debtor nation in the world? Why did we not vote with the government? It is because we believed, as we do today, that the government's approach was wrong. The government's approach was to surrender in the face of unemployment.
We do not believe in the so-called war against inflation and that 1.6 million unemployed across this country or nearly three million underemployed are acceptable losses-to use a Vietnam kind of wording-in the war against inflation. We have been saying that for a number of years. We have not been listened to.
This economic experiment where all bend down before the altar of so-called unshackled capitalism as proposed by this government has failed. It has failed.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
In Great Britain where Margaret Thatcher held sway the country is in a mess. In a recent Gallup poll more than 50 per cent of the people of Great Britain said that if they had the opportunity they would leave Great Britain.
In the United States where Ronald Reagan held sway with his so-called revolution the debt of that country has been driven through the roof. Those who were fundamentally dishonest have profited. The savings and loans scandal was unvarnished greed where people took the pension funds, the retirement funds and the savings of the innocent.
They created phoney corporations and this was all done legally under the Republican's new U.S. law. They ripped off hundreds of millions and billions. They ran with the cash and left innocent people bankrupt. The American government bailed them out. That same right wing philosophy prevailed here and got us in trouble.
We bailed out the banks. We are spending almost $6 billion on helicopters because some lobbyist is making a mint off the commission but we will not put one nickel on the table to put an unemployed Canadian back to work.
The government will not even ask our people who are begging for a chance to participate with us in a crusade for our country. Canadians know this is a great country. They just want a government and a plan that knows it as well. They want a chance to rebuild this great land.

Mr. Speaker, we hear so much being spoken about the helicopters and the cost of these helicopters. Opposition members do not take into account that the amount of money which is $4.6 billion in 1992 dollars will be spent over 13 years. That is quite different from what is being quoted all the time.
There are 800 helicopters presently on order in the world and Canada will have 10 per cent of every helicopter built. It will also create 45,000 person-year jobs for Canadians. I think this is something we have to put down. There is job creation and that is very important.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member made her comments sincerely but I want to tell her there are not 800 helicopters on order world-wide.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: Yes, there are.

I am giving you the facts. There are 70 on order world-wide and 50 were ordered by Canada alone. We are ordering more of those helicopters than all the rest of the planet combined, including the two countries that are building them. The member opposite, whom I have known for a long time, should check her facts before she says it is not true.
Members opposite are sensitive about these helicopters because they are going to bring this party and this government crashing back down to earth.
Canadians know a multimillion dollar job to fill the pockets of lobbyists when they see it. The only people who are going to profit from this are Tory lobbyists.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the rest of the debate can be conducted without these histrionics because I do not think they are helpful to Canadians who are concerned, as I know a number of my friends opposite are, where we are going vis-a-vis the deficit and the debt. People are interested in the future of our country want to see a responsible method taken to reduce the deficit and the debt. They want to see something concrete and some real plans.
I regret that while a lot is being said on the other side about what is wrong with this budget, I see very little productive or positive comments coming from them and no suggestion or plan that would give Canadians confidence. The fact of the matter is they do not have a plan and they do not have any new ideas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well neither do you in this budget. This is all old stuff. Nobody else thinks this is good either.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would say that the budget of April 26, 1993 is now before us and this is what we are dealing with, not old stuff. We are dealing with the future and what is going on in the country today.
April 27, 1993

It is no surprise-you have been listening to it all day-when I say the budget has not met with universal approval. Canada would not be Canada if it had and the opposition would not be the opposition if it approved of anything the government did because members of the opposition are very hungry for power these days.
Although they do not have any real plan or any real idea of what they might do with that power, we can smell the greed and hunger over there. It is affecting and impacting their judgment and it often impacts on what they are saying.
While it is easy for the opposition to criticize, I think it would be much more difficult to be in the finance minister's resoled shoes. The hon. finance minister did not go out and buy a new pair of shoes in honour of what is happening these days in the economy. He had his current shoes resoled. I would say it is much more difficult to be in his shoes than it is to sit on the other side of the House and criticize indiscriminately simply for the sake of opposing.
I really want to extend my very sympathetic understanding to my colleague, the hon. Minister of Finance. He had some very tough choices to make and he was faced with bringing down a budget very close to an election and of course close to a change in leadership. He is doing this at a time when our options are so few. I congratulate him, as my colleague the Minister of the Environment pointed out, for setting the table for the next leadership convention and the election that is coming. He is setting the table for a renewed mandate for the Conservative government. I think he has done an admirable job under these circumstances and once again I extend my congratulations to him.
The opposition has made a great to-do this morning about the fact it did not see anything in the budget to stimulate the economy. I want to set the record straight by pointing out that this budget is an adjunct to the financial statement that was made in December which contained many provisions to stimulate the economy. I see my friend opposite does not want to hear this so he is leaving. He is blocking out what I say and ignoring it because the truth is very difficult for him to take. I can understand that. Nevertheless I am going to say this
The Budget
anyway for his edification. Perhaps he will be good enough to read the record later.
We have taken measures to support the recovery and let me just list some of them. There has been a reduction in the personal income surtax which is already in effect. It has put more money in the pockets of Canadians in those provinces that did not take that money back and use it for their own purposes. Certainly in my province, Manitoba, the tax reduction was allowed to stand and Manitobans now have more money as a result of the initiative taken by the federal government.
We have also introduced a two-year special home-buyer's plan which is in effect. There have been other things like a reduction in manufacturing and processing tax rates and an increase in the CCA for manufacturing and processing machinery and equipment. We have redirected capital gains exemptions. We have streamlined research and development tax credits and made changes to the withholding tax.
We have done a number of other things and I will not go into all of the detail, but just in case my friends opposite want to bring this up I can tell them that much has been done to stimulate the recovery in Canada and it is paying off. We are seeing the impact now. The economy is growing and has been doing so for seven consecutive quarters. Clearly we are past the recession and now on to a steady rate of growth.
In this budget there is a long list of measures that will be very positive for Canada. We will save $3.8 billion in this fiscal year of 1993-94 and this is important for the short term. We will not raise taxes or add new taxes. We will further simplify the GST remittance system for small businesses which is important to their competitiveness and their ability to reduce the cost of doing business.
One of the highlights in the non-monetary measures carried in this budget is the further reduction of regulations so small businesses will be able to find a level playing-field and remove obstacles to their competitiveness. The happy result is that in addition to saving small business money we are also going to save the taxpayer money because the cost of administration will come down when, out of the 700 regulations we examine, we abandon one out of every four. That is the kind of positive initiative that organizations like the Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Council of National Business have been requesting for a long time. They know

April 27, 1993
The Budget
that the paper burden and regulation for the sake of regulation reduce Canada's competitive position and make it difficult for us to take full advantage of the economic recovery opportunities that are out there waiting for us as we pull out of this recession.
We will also do something that will help individuals. I have had many people talk to me about the tax system that requires quarterly tax instalments. That will now be modified and about 300,000 tax filers will be exempt from having to file their tax claims on a quarterly basis. That will affect mainly seniors with lower incomes. At the same time it will also save us some money.
In addition to that we are going to send out GST rebates twice a year instead of four times a year. That will reduce the administrative costs to the tune of about $7.5 million a year. All of these sensible, careful measures are designed to improve our competitive position and reduce the costs of budgeting and administering our government. This is just a small example of the many progressive measures contained in this budget and I heartily applaud them.
I also applaud the winding up of eight redundant government agencies and the merging of four more. I urge that the planned privatization of the targeted Crown corporations be accomplished with all good haste because that will save us even more money.
I am also delighted to see the rationalization of program spending in the provincial jurisdictions of mining and forestry. These are sensible measures that will make this government more efficient and more responsive to the needs of the 1990s. It is time the federal government got out of provincial jurisdiction because we simply cannot afford to duplicate services and compete with one another when there is only one taxpayer out there and only one tax dollar to spend.
In spite of all this, I must say that given the national psyche that currently understands the very real imperatives of the debt, I think with some regret of what my hon. colleague might have done if the circumstances had been different and we were not at the end of a mandate, for example.
I think of the directions a new leader must be prepared to give the finance minister as early as this fall after the coming election. Real change will have to take place in the way we do the business of government, not just federally here in Ottawa but at all levels of government. Real change will also have to take place in the way people look at government and what they expect of government. Perhaps some of our sacred cows will have to be led to the slaughterhouse as we look for ways to cope with the deficit and debt.
Governments can no longer be all things to all people. We can no longer set ourselves up as our brother's keeper, taking care of people's concerns from the cradle to the grave, because we simply do not have the resources to do it. The prosperity that we thought we were enjoying in the 1970s and the early 1980s was a false prosperity based on borrowing that we did on our children's future. That must now come to an end as it always ultimately had to.
Now we must change our way of doing things and our way of looking at things. Canadians must take responsibility for their own destinies. They must understand it is not a question of what their government can do for them. The question is: what is my responsibility to myself, my participation in democracy and my fellow Canadians? How productive can I be? What can I contribute? Because it is through contribution, productivity and getting involved in helping out that we realize the full benefit of our citizenship in this wonderful country. Attitudes will have to change.
While I applaud the work of my colleague, the Minister of Finance, I want to pause for a moment to consider other possibilities. For example, this budget allows the provincial governments to continue to increase their spending at a rate of 4 per cent per year while the federal government will restrain its increases to 1.5 per cent a year, even though we expect inflation to run somewhere between 1.5 per cent and 2.5 per cent. That means no real spending federally and no real spending growth.
I ask Canadians to consider whether or not the provincial governments can continue to increase their expenditures at the rate of 4 per cent growth when we are facing this very serious and real situation vis-a-vis our total national debt. I think the provinces must take responsibility along with the federal government and the
April 27, 1993

municipalities and come together to work on these problems as a single unit rather than each going its own way because that is taking us to perdition.
If we had reduced the provincial transfers to the same rate of growth as the rest of our budget we would save $9 billion over the next five years. Coincidentally, that is about the same amount as our budgetary shortfall this year in terms of our expectations of revenues. It is a serious amount of money and I think that while we are dealing with this year's budget, if we look over the next five years I would suggest to provincial finance ministers that they begin to examine ways to cut their own expenditures in very real terms so they do not have to accept growth in transfer payments from the taxpayer who is sending part of his money to the federal government. At some point or other, if we do not get this under control, tax increases will be absolutely necessary and nobody wants that to happen, least of all the federal government.
When the finance ministers come together, as the federal Minister of Finance has pledged they will do, and I think that is a very positive thing, they are going to be forced to come to the very same conclusion that most Canadians have already reached. That is that there is only one taxpayer, regardless of how many levels of government there are, and the taxpayer is saying: "Enough is enough. Get your fiscal house in order. Do it decisively and do it now."
The budget proposes to cut grants and contributions 10 per cent this year and 10 per cent next year. It promises further reductions of 15 per cent in 1995 and 1996 and 20 per cent thereafter. That is very good and positive.
At the same time we are exempting a long list of programs such as transfers for individuals receiving veterans and Old Age Security benefits, the Canadian Jobs Strategy, selected native programs, famine relief and programs for the disabled. This is gentle and humane treatment as indeed it should be because it is part of our job to look after the vulnerable.
In addition to that we are exempting granting agencies, such as the Canada Council. Their budgets, as well as the budgets of university granting councils will be kept to the same rate of increase, 1.5 per cent, as other government spending.
The Budget
In addition, grants and contributions affecting science and technology will receive favourable treatment. I approve of that because education has to be one of our highest priorities. In fact, all of these things are high on our priority list and I respect the thinking that went into the exemptions.
However we must begin to think about our future priorities and how they will be funded. We have to make some decisions about whether or not we as Canadians are willing to give up some of our cherished but perhaps non-essential programs in order to preserve funding for things like education and health.
I noticed as the debate proceeded this morning and members opposite stood in their places and spoke, that while they had a great deal of criticism on the cuts made in this particular budget and the measures that have been taken, they had very little to offer as alternatives. They did not tell us what programs they would cut or how they would decrease their expenditures without hurting individuals.
People across the country are calling out for even deeper cuts because they are concerned about what is going to happen in the future. They are demanding that contributions to advocacy groups and other special interest groups be eliminated altogether. People are telling us that unless a program can be shown to have a net benefit to a large number of Canadians, we should not be funding it. People are saying that we all have to become more self-reliant, we have to become more independent. People are also saying that they are really tired of robbing Peter to pay an ever-greedy and hungry Paul whose rich diet is making him too heavy to carry himself alone.
I know the finance minister is a very kind and gentle man who wants to ease the pain of these cuts by making them gradually. That is why the bulk of the announced savings of $30 billion is scheduled to occur in years three, four and five. We are delighted, as I said before, to learn that there will be no new taxes and no additional taxes as a result of this budget.
I am still concerned however that our debt will continue to grow. Even with a $30 billion savings by 1997-98 we will see the debt grow to over $563 billion. This is in spite of the good news that the deficit will be reduced by then to $8 billion on an anticipated gross domestic product of $928 billion.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
I believe it is very much a question of priorities that Canadians must continue to address. In this budget, for example, we speak about constraining annual growth in government spending on international assistance by limiting increases to 1.5 per cent beginning in 1994-95. That is after taking into account the 10 per cent decreases announced in December for the coming year of 1993-94. As I said earlier, famine relief is exempted. Given the very real difficulties that many countries face, this move may seem to be somewhat harsh and it certainly is regrettable. However, I would suggest that if we do not get our finances in order we will no longer be able to borrow the money with which to support these initiatives.
On balance, this budget is a lot less painful than many of us had hoped and perhaps others had feared. It is true that the full impact has not yet been analysed. After all, $3.9 billion in expenditure cuts is not insignificant. Of course, $30 billion is even more significant. I must emphasize the importance of meeting and even exceeding these expenditure reductions in the coming five years.
Experience tells us that the fine people over at the Department of Finance have a very long history of budgetary optimism. They do not have unfortunately a particularly good record of predicting revenues.
I urge caution in accepting the premises that tell us to expect a growth rate of 4.6 per cent in 1994. I have not crunched the numbers, but I question the wisdom of bucking the consensus of private sector outlooks by rejecting a growth projection of 4 per cent and the premise that expects the gap between real output to narrow to 5.5 per cent by 1994 and close to 1.75 per cent by 1998.
There are some really big questions we have to ask ourselves: will inflation average out at 1.5 per cent over the medium term? Will employment fall to 7.5 per cent by the end of 1998? These are some concerns that I would like to voice as we look optimistically ahead on a five-year plan. There are just too many unknowns and intangibles, not the least of which is an unprecedented acceleration in technological change and a bulge in the age of the work force which was trained to meet employment patterns of two and three decades ago.
We must focus our minds on the changes we are making for this year and ask if they are going to save our credibility on the international money markets. That is what is important right now. I suggest that they are.
Perhaps the most important message sent yesterday is the one that promises an all-out attempt by the federal government to find a co-operative approach with the provinces in future budget setting. No government can act in isolation of others in the 1990s. Our competitive position will depend on our ability to act cohesively, to tackle our problems together as Canadians and not as a rag-tag assortment of political entities acting as though they were independent of one another and of the federal government. We must all work together to keep our country whole.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have expected my colleague to support her government's budget. I do not criticize that, but she did ask one question: what will the opposition do besides criticize? We suggested that we could cancel the helicopter project and perhaps invest in an infrastructure program for improving the sewers, roads and the other things of our cities and towns that improve the quality of life.
I want to ask my colleague some specific questions. What will this budget do for the 1.6 million unemployed Canadians, for the 2.7 million Canadians receiving social assistance, for the more than two million Canadians using food banks? I do not say that critically. It is an important question to me. How will this help them? What will it do for the middle class which is really the motor of the Canadian economy? If the middle class is suffering, then clearly the economic performance of the country will not be as good as it might be.
My final question is more specific to Manitoba. What will be the impact of this budget with respect to the cuts being imposed on regional development, the cuts with respect to VIA Rail, the cuts with respect to CBC, the cuts with respect to the mining and forestry agreements? These will all have negative job impacts in Manitoba. I am wondering if my hon. colleague would care to respond to those specific questions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always appreciate the intelligent questions of my colleague opposite. I will try to answer them; I hope I got them all down.
April 27, 1993

The Budget
He asked about the helicopters and he talked about infrastructure spending. I suggest to my hon. colleague that in fact helicopters are part of our infrastructure. Our ability to protect our coastal waters, to manage search and rescue missions, to ensure that we have integrity in the north and sovereignty are dependent on our ability to have helicopters that do not fall out of the sky because they have aged beyond the point of no return. Spending on helicopters is spending on part of the infrastructure. I would point out as my colleague mentioned not that long ago, that the money which is being spent on the helicopters, some $4.5 billion, is not being spent in one year. It is being spent over a period of 13 years. I think the impact on the budget is far less important than people may believe.
The hon. member also asked what we are doing to help with the question of employment. That is a very difficult and serious question. There are many pressures right now on the marketplace. They have to do not just with the fact that we have gone through a recession, but that we are going through some fundamental restructuring in our economy and some fundamental restructuring in the way we do business throughout the world. Part of that has to do with technological change as well as the economic restructuring. Another part of it has to do here in Canada with the fact that we have a lot more competition for jobs. Forty-five per cent of women work and that places competition and competitive stresses on traditional entrant into the work force.
We have taken measures in the December economic statement to ensure that the economy will move forward in a productive way and that recovery will gather momentum. If these predictions are correct-and I do have the same doubts I am sure my hon. friend does about predictions for five years-but if correct, unemployment will be reduced by 7.5 per cent at the end of five years. I assure the hon. member that if this government is in office it will continue to do everything it can to accelerate the pace of that change.
The hon. member also asked what this budget will do for the middle class. Again, making sure that we have our fiscal house in order is part of ensuring that our middle class, which is the largest contributor to our coffers, has an infrastructure, a government in place that
is rational and controls its deficits and leaves some options and some choices open.
As far as real spending on programs to improve conditions for the unemployed or improve conditions for the middle class, my friend must know that the options right now are extremely limited. It is a choice again of from whom do you steal to pay the other fellow. I suggest that getting the economy in order and making sure that jobs are being created, as in fact they are on a daily basis as the economy begins to grow, will do more for the middle class and the unemployed than any artificial stimulus the government might create.
Finally, the hon. member asks about cuts in Manitoba. Last night that question was asked in my presence and in the presence of Mr. Manness, the minister of finance in Manitoba. His response was the best one. He said clearly that as long as these expenditure reductions were fairly spread across the provinces he had no complaint because all of us must do our part.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question prefaced by a couple of quick comments for the member for Winnipeg South. I understand that we have differing views of priorities and what is right, coming from different philosophies, but we accept those even though we may argue about them from time to time.
In one case in order to defend what I firmly believe is the indefensible in this budget, the member said that the federal government was getting out of the forestry agreements because it was an example of governments competing with each other. That seemed to be the suggestion.
Maybe coming from Winnipeg she is not as aware as some other members of the nature of these agreements. They started back in 1983 I think with John Roberts in the former Liberal administration. It was a one-year program, $55 million a year from the federal government and $55 million from the province in the case of B.C.
When the present government assumed office in 1984, the gentleman who is still Minister of Forestry, who was the author of The Green Ghetto prior to that, did something that was good. He spent less money annually but got better results by negotiating these jointly administered, jointly funded agreements and got more bang for the buck. This allowed the provinces and the federal government by working together to accomplish much

April 27, 1993
The Budget
more with less money than was the case when it was done on the short term. I simply cannot understand her reference to these kinds of jointly negotiated, jointly funded, jointly administered agreements, as governments competing with each other. It is one of the best investments I have seen during all the time I have been a member of this place or simply been interested in the forestry industry or the political sphere.
It strikes me as almost an insult to the present minister when he has announced that he is leaving parliamentary life, to eliminate the federal government's share in a program that has returned more and demanded more money if we are to fulfil any commitment to the green plan or the principle of sustainable development. I believe in this case she was defending the indefensible. I would like to ask her to try to justify it or perhaps tell me that I was wrong in my interpretation of what she said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do appreciate the question. I think it is a valid one and I am glad it was raised.
The fact is that programs of this nature are not created to last forever. They do not and should not replace the natural and normal condition that would prevail, which is that forestry is a provincial jurisdiction as are all other resources. Constitutionally it is not appropriate for the federal government to spend a long time in a field like forestry.
In addition to that there are some practical implications here. There was competition, duplication and in some cases resentment because of the occupation of this field by the federal government. Not that long ago I had the occasion to be with the minister of forestry in Manitoba, actually the Minister of Natural Resources because he deals with more than forests. He pointed out to me that while he was the minister responsible for all the forests in Manitoba, he had fewer foresters in the province than did the federal Minister of Forestry, and the federal Minister of Forestry had no responsibility for forests in the province of Manitoba.
While the short-term program may have had a very beneficial effect in some areas, and certainly in my area because we do have forestry and logging and I have lumber companies in my own riding, there has to be a sunset clause on these programs. We have to back out of them when the expenditure can no longer be justified according to the long waiting list of priorities that is out there for the dollars that are available.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that I was not here yesterday to listen to the minister's speech. I was at a nomination meeting in Essex-Windsor which had been scheduled long before and could not be changed. However I must say that if there has been any budget to miss in the eight and a half years of Conservative government, any budget that one could somehow nod through and not have missed a thing, it is this budget. Aside from having an awful lot of propaganda trying to prop up failed records, this budget has absolutely nothing in it. It has no new ideas of any sort and no new initiatives. We were told that the guillotine was coming down in this budget and there was going to be a serious attempt to get control of the deficit situation in this country.
What do we find? Absolutely nothing, except a little bit of creative bookkeeping which puts the GST tax rebate for next year into the next fiscal year by paying people twice a year instead of four times a year.
That represents $625 million in savings out of the $1 billion in savings that is supposedly in this budget.
We have just been talking about the forestry industry and I must say I am struck with horror when I think of the budget and the number of trees that have been sacrificed to produce this piece of absolutely empty nonsense. It is just tragic.
We have an economic crisis here in Canada in 1993. We have 11 per cent of our population out of work, according to the official figures. A real measure of the unemployment rate might be calculated by asking how many people really want to work. We might go back and find the participation rate in the economy in a province where there was a fair amount of economic activity, like Ontario, in the period just before the recession hit in early 1990. The participation rate was about 70.1 per cent at that stage. If we were to apply that participation rate now to the whole country, and surely it is fair to do so because that is a measure of the number of people who wanted to work then and who want to work now, we see that over 17 per cent of the people in this country are unemployed. We are talking about a national catastrophe.
There has been a lot of hoo-ha about a debt crisis. The biggest debt crisis we have in this country is the one this government suffers from when it comes to ideas and compassion for those who are out of work. It exhibits an absolutely abysmal lack of care.
April 27, 1993

With that number of people out of work, the government brings forward a budget that has absolutely nothing in it to try to help those who are out of work. We have seen previous budgets that have had in my view a set of unfortunate initiatives, but usually in every case it has been possible to point to at least one or two areas where the minister of the day has tried to show some political or economic initiative to deal with the unemployment problem in Canada.
There is not even the pretence of that in this budget. There is nothing here whatsoever. You can start with the summary of the Minister of Finance about all the great things that are in this budget: "No new taxes, no tax increases. More than $30 billion in spending cuts and other measures." Of course, the spending cuts are all in the future. They do not affect the present.
There are all sort of things but not one single point is mentioned about what is going to be done about the serious problem of unemployment in Canada. In fact the only thing that is in this budget which deals with unemployment is an extension of the reduction in unemployment benefits for unemployed people into the future.
It is a heartless government that has lost touch with the realities in this country.
I stood up in the House last week in an Opposition Day debate and listed, from my constituency alone, close to 3,000 workers who had lost their jobs through the dozens of plant shutdowns that have taken place in the Windsor area. Is there anything in this budget that attempts to respond to the concerns of those people? There is not a thing.
In addition, we have to say there are some usual petty, nasty, wicked little hooks in this budget as there have been in every Conservative budget that has been produced since this government came into power.
In this case it has taken the GST rebate which goes to poorer families in this country who were promised it
The Budget
would be given four times a year to offset the increased burden of the GST and said: "We are going to do away with four times a year. We are going to make it just twice a year." There is no recognition of the increased problems that will cause for poorer families in Canada.
On top of it all, these great deficit fighters on the other side of the aisle have brought forward in their last budget a deficit that is higher than the deficit they projected for their first budget in 1985. In other words, we have had almost nine years of Conservative rule in this country by people who are mesmerized by the deficit. Despite all its rhetoric, fuming, excuses and close to 40 new taxes it has put into effect to hit Canadians, the government has to project a higher deficit in its last budget than it could project in its first budget in 1985.
Mind you it is consistent with previous Conservative budgets too. This budget, like all Conservative budgets since 1985 is really good at dealing with the deficit problem five years down the road. If we believe in Alice in Wonderland and like to read our kids fairy stories we could find all sorts of material in this budget. Suddenly, miraculously, the Canadian economy is going to start growing at 4.5 per cent per year. It does not say how. It is going to happen. It will be 4.5 per cent per year.
This remarkable, miraculous growth is going to create a reduction in the deficit. Suddenly by 1998, safely down the road, the borrowing requirements of this government are going to be eliminated. This is the first step toward eliminating the deficit.
It is funny. If you go back to the first budget of the Conservatives in 1985, they were going to have reached that no borrowing position by this year, 1993. Here we are in 1993 and what do we have? We have a bigger deficit than in the first year that the Conservatives presented a budget.
Talk about mismanagement, talk about the tooth fairy, talk about Alice in Wonderland. Anybody who believes the statistics presented in this budget needs to be taken to the Clarke Institute in Toronto and given an extensive series of shock treatments.

April 27, 1993
The reality is that there is virtually nothing in this budget that will help with any of Canada's problems whatsoever. I have to admit there is one good thing that I have managed to find in the course of 94 pages, one good point. That is the suggestion that we should merge the National Advisory Council on Aging and the National Council of Welfare. That makes sense, but the government says it is also going to do away with all sorts of other committees which it turns out do not have any members anyway so it is awfully easy to get rid of them. That does not prove very much.
It is a budget without a hope of doing anything to help people in this country. By bringing this budget forward at this time the Conservatives have lost the chance in the final budget they will present, I hope for a generation, to keep some of the promises they made, such as the promise to set up a national child care program.
I had people speaking with me this morning from child care advocacy groups across this country, not just the parents but some of the children who have benefited so much from national child care efforts in the past in Canada. They left me some of their very well-presented propaganda. It makes the case very well that we need a national child care program in this country. We need a program to put people to work in the child care area but above all we need a program that will help children by providing high quality child care throughout Canada.
Our New Democrat jobs program makes a commitment to such a child care program for Canada but this government, despite its promises in the last election, has refused to come through.
This government promised to help small business, but again it has not done so. We have argued that we need a national investment fund in this country for Canadian-owned businesses so they would have access to the capital they need to expand their activities through venture capital.
We have argued for a commitment to work force training. We have argued for encouragement of employee ownership where feasible and tightened research requirements on foreign investment. All of those things could have been part of this budget without any extra expenditure of money in many cases. Yet there are no
new ideas, no new initiatives, and no new hope for Canada's unemployed.
I wonder if I could call it two o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an article published in the newspaper Les Affaires of April 17, 1993, says that "the federal government delivered the goods in Quebec, through the Canada-Quebec agreement on regional development."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are longing for a revival of confidence in their country, renewed hope for their future and brighter prospects for their children. On farms, in small towns, in factories and in homes Canadians expect better for the 39 new taxes they have faced under this government than they received yesterday.
April 27, 1993

This government cannot seem to grasp that it is not a question of more government or less government but of good government. It is a question of effective public services delivered at a price the country can afford by a Public Service that has the talent and tools it needs to do the job that Parliament has told it to do.
This calculator budgeting that comes up with arbitrary percentage or dollar cuts simply is not delivering the value that Canadians expect for the increased taxes they are going to continue paying into the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I met with a number of outstanding but distraught young athletes who are members of our national speed skating team. They expressed to me their dismay that their coach, Jack Walters, had been fired by the Canadian Amateur Speed Skating Association.
Throughout the past 20 years, 12 of which he spent coaching Gaetan Boucher, Jack Walters has earned the respect and admiration of the national and international speed skating community as one of the world's finest coaches.
This extraordinary reputation is due to the mutual trust, confidence and respect between him and his athletes, outstanding results and his willingness to share his progressive and innovative ideas among the national and international community of coaches.
Canadian taxpayers pay 70 per cent to 75 per cent of the Canadian Amateur Speed Skating Association's costs. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past nine years the Conservative government
has asked us to make sacrifices in order to fight the federal deficit and the federal debt, help future generations, develop a globally competitive economy and improve our quality of life, and we have.
Canadians placed their trust in this government. Since the Conservatives took office in 1984 the federal debt has more than doubled to $460 billion. They have consistently posted annual deficits in the $30 billion range. The tax burden on the hard working middle class family has increased to 44 per cent of their income. Over 1.5 million Canadians are unemployed, among them are over 430,000 young people; 30 per cent of our high school students continue to drop out; 2.2 million live on welfare; 2 million rely on food banks; and violent crime has gone up 40 per cent. Tory times are tough times.

speakerposition: subtopic
Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the real failure of this government is that it does not understand what truly holds Canada together. Our national institutions make this country viable, institutions like the CBC which allows us to learn about each other, VIA Rail which enables us to visit each other and Canada Post which allows us to communicate with each other.
Yesterday's budget makes it obvious that the Tories are plotting the death of VIA Rail. These latest cuts will force VIA to cut routes and services and make it much more difficult for VIA to acquire the new equipment it will soon need just to function.
While VIA officials will work hard to minimize the effects of these cuts, there is no question that the lower the ongoing investment in rail passenger service the smaller and less frequent VIA will become. This country is too big to leave the funding of rail passenger service to the marketplace.
If we are to continue to have rail passenger service from coast to coast the Canadian government has a role to play. It is not constitutions that keep this country together but people communicating with each other by radio, by television, by letter and through transportation that is affordable and accessible.

April 27, 1993

Mr. Speaker, the Ships Company Theatre was established several years ago in the town of Parrsboro, Nova Scotia. Its impact has been felt throughout the Parrsboro shore as it attracts people from several provinces nearby.
It is established in a dry-docked ferry boat called the Kipawa which creates a unique atmosphere and is very conducive to the setting and appropriate to the productions.
The Parrsboro shore area is now experiencing a small boom in tourism and this theatre group was the main original building block which helped to attract many of the other tourism facilities under construction.
The Ships Company Theatre is now applying to the federal government, the provincial government, and the municipality for assistance in funding to allow it to continue to survive and prosper.
Canada Employment has recently announced a section 25 grant to help it upgrade its facilities, which is a start. Applications will be made to ACOA and the Department of Communications, as well as to the province, to assist with a relatively small amount of funding to ensure this continues.
I strongly support the Ships Company Theatre in its efforts to resolve its financial challenges and will be endorsing its applications whole-heartedly.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday's budget was good news for senior citizens in my constituency and across Canada. Currently an individual must remit quarterly income tax instalments if both their prior year and current year federal tax liability is more than $1,000 and less than three-quarters of their current year's net income is subject to withholding tax at source.
Effective September 15, 1994, an individual will be required to pay instalments only if the difference between the tax payable and the amount withheld at source is greater than $2,000 in both the current and either of the two preceding years.
This means that some 300,000 people, a great many of them seniors, will no longer be required to make quarterly income tax instalment payments. That is great news for seniors.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's economic future is in grave doubt. Since 1984 manufacturing productivity has grown at only two-thirds the rate of the G-7 and under this government our high-tech trade has fallen from a surplus of $1 billion to a $30 billion deficit.
Since 1989 we have fallen from fourth to eleventh place in the world in terms of our ability to compete. We have lost 16 per cent of our manufacturing jobs and our unemployment rate is stuck at 11 per cent.
Yesterday the government's challenge was to offer policies to help Canada compete as a high-wage nation and create jobs. It failed to address our deficiencies in education, training, numeracy, literacy, science and technology, and research and development.
It offered nothing to help small businesses expand, to assist manufacturers with productivity, exports and quality, or to help our primary industries add value here in Canada.
This budget is a prescription for our continuing economic decline. This government continues to fail us miserably.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada for its innovative and dynamic approach toward the safety of older consumers during this National Consumer Week.
We should keep in mind that each year over 3,000 seniors die and over 67,000 more are hospitalized as a result of an injury. In 1986 injury related expenditures were estimated at $11 billion and injuries are currently the second leading health care problem. Injuries involving consumer products are of particular concern to seniors because of the severe impact they have on their quality of life.
April 27, 1993

As the Canadian population continues to age the number of injuries and related deaths and associated health costs will significantly increase.
The department has introduced initiatives to reduce product related injuries suffered by seniors in their homes. It is working with industry and seniors' groups to make industry aware of the product and packaging needs of the seniors.
The Canadian Seniors Packaging Advisory Council, CSPAC, was established to address seniors' packaging needs. A national working group was formed to promote products of universal design. Such consumer products will make life easier not only for seniors but also for all Canadians.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Monday's budget this government announced that it will not renew the federal-provincial economic and regional development agreements in the areas of forestry and mineral resource development. This is bad news for Canadians who rely on the mining and forestry industries.
In Manitoba this announcement means the loss of $5 million in federal funding for mineral development and $15 million for forestry. How does the government think that Manitoba and the other provinces will make up this difference?
Although the federal government has not given up its constitutional obligation to forestry and mining these cuts reduce any federal influence in these important areas. The federal government has a role to play in the forestry and mining industries. The government's decision to pull out of these areas is disgraceful and will hurt thousands of working people and hundreds of communities right across Canada.

speakerposition: subtopic
Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:

This year the federal government is highlighting the importance of consumer credit during National Consumer Week so that consumers can act with full knowledge when they use the credit options available to them.
It seems clear that the marketplace conditions affecting the use of credit have undergone fundamental changes and that these conditions are likely to persist. For example, while some types of consumer debts have declined from their recent peak level the use of consumer credit is still more common than it was a decade ago.
Another change involves the misuse of credit and particularly credit cards. To address this problem, there is a need for more informational and educational initiatives which will reduce levels of serious indebtedness and, in some cases, prevent personal bankruptcies.
As this is a complex and serious matter, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is communicating his concerns to the provinces and credit grantors. He is asking them to provide their ideas on how problems of excessive indebtedness can be prevented and how the importance of the wise use of credit can be effectively communicated to consumers.
In addition to co-operative action with provincial governments and credit grantors we will continue-

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's budget was an abominable insult to Canadians and a pathetic attempt at deficit reduction.
In fact the budget will increase spending by $13.4 billion over the next three years, if the Conservative Party is around after the next election to implement the necessary legislation.
Are Canadians supposed to get excited about the fact that there were no new taxes? This is little consolation for the average working man and woman who have seen their taxes rise by 26.7 per cent since these deficit dragoons took power in 1984.
What Canadians need is not a stay the course, do-nothing cop-out but a real deficit reduction budget from a real government.
