April 27, 1993

speakerposition: subtopic
Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget tabled by the Minister of Finance yesterday is a useless and meaningless budget which does nothing to remedy unemployment or poverty.
Again, the minister is attacking the old and the poor. The GST credit is currently paid four times a year but, come January, families expecting to receive their cheque as usual from the government will have to wait another three months.
Such a measure is nothing more than an accounting trick and it unfairly penalizes low-income families. The government had promised that the GST credit would be paid often, sometimes even ahead of time to help those in need.
I think this measure is unfair and I ask the Minister of Finance to withdraw it.

speakerposition: topic
subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
After years of double digit unemployment and with 1.5 million Canadians still looking for work the best the government can do in its budget is to have 11 per cent unemployment this year and about the same level next year.
I ask the minister: where is the plan for economic growth and job creation that would bring unemployment down substantially this year and next? Will the minister admit the reason he does not have a plan for jobs in his budget is that it is designed to help the political needs of the Conservative Party and not the economic needs of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a realistic, responsible and achievable budget. It builds on the initiatives of the December statement to bolster growth and to invest in people and infrastructure. I draw attention to the economic statement wherein it indicates that in fiscal year 1993-94 some $1.1 billion will be spent
Oral Questions
on bolstering the economy. In 1994-95 there is another $1 billion.
The personal income tax reductions and the child benefit credit inject $1.7 billion into the economy this year. We have in place a special two-year home buyer's plan. We have reduced the manufacturing and processing tax rate. We have increased the capital cost allowance for manufacturing and processing. We have streamlined research and development. We have removed the withholding taxes.
We announced an infrastructure program that is generating 15,000 person-years of work now and another
15,000	in the future. We have provided measures to assist small business. We have increased the business loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act. We have provided UI premium relief for new jobs. We have a small business investment tax credit.
All of these initiatives are taking hold and have created 200,000 new full-time jobs since August.

And after all this, Mr. Speaker, the minister in his own budget says that unemployment will remain at the tragically high level of 11 per cent this year and 10.6 per cent next year. Is that not an admission of failure?
My supplementary question to the minister is this: today the Prime Minister's office announced a detailed plan for the Prime Minister's farewell tour of Europe. Why is it possible for the government to design a detailed plan for this farewell tour and impossible for the government to design a detailed plan in its budget to quickly put 1.5 million Canadians back to work?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will give you an idea of the seriousness of the ideas on the other side of the House.
As Prime Minister of Canada, I have accepted an invitation from President Yeltsin to visit with him in Russia in respect of the G-7's attempts to contribute to the stabilization of the former Soviet Union. Canada's per capita contribution is second only to that of Germany and our arrangements for the Vancouver summit have been with that in mind.
Our meetings with Chancellor Kohl deal principally with the reignition of the GATT talks and their impor-

April 27, 1993
Oral Questions
tance to Canada. The new Prime Minister of France, Edouard Balladur, has invited us, given the importance of France to Canada, particularly in regard to our foreign policy. These are important and significant steps to take.
I find it difficult to understand that my hon. friend, as a Privy Councillor and a member of a former government whose Prime Minister in 1984 took trips to Romania, East Germany and half-way around the world, would seek to trivialize an important initiative on behalf of the Government of Canada.
If my hon. friend has some better ideas in regard to the budget, let him bring them forward but he should not try to trivialize Canada's important initiatives in foreign policy in this manner.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister seems uncommonly sensitive about this point. I am wondering if he is going to take Mr. McCutchan with him. That would be some proof that it is a serious trip.

Mr. Speaker, my third question is directed to the Minister of Finance. In its budget, the government plans to spend $5.8 billion to buy military helicopters while at the same time making drastic cuts in social housing and regional development. I want to ask the minister why this government has such a distorted sense of priorities? Why?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member looks at the expenditure cut projections, he will find that there are some $5.9 billion worth of expenditure cuts to the Department of National Defence budget. If that is taken over the period from 1989-90 right through until 1997-98, it will be found that there have been cuts of some $14 billion in the defence budget. I think that is pretty substantial.
Clearly with respect to social housing, we are still going to be supporting social housing at the level of some $2 billion. Any new housing initiatives will have to be funded out of expenditures that are available for that given year. We cannot continue to provide the 35-year subsidy provision that layers up the cost exposure and establishes a liability for future generations. Every $40
million worth of investment in social housing works out to about $1.5 billion worth of exposure.
These are some of the things we have had to deal with. We have to live within our means and we have to adjust the mechanisms and the institutions available to deal with the reality of severe fiscal restraint.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Everybody recognizes that small and medium-sized businesses are the main vehicles of growth and job creation in Canada. This budget was the last chance for this government to make a concrete proposal to our business people but it failed to seize that opportunity.
Once again, why did the Minister of Finance refuse to suggest an action plan allowing Canadians and small and medium-sized businesses to develop new products, export them all over the world, and win the global economic battle?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is quite aware of the initiatives we took in the December statement.
I repeat that this budget builds upon the efforts in the December statement both in terms of policy and in terms of expenditure reduction. I might add that those expenditure reductions enunciated in the December statement have been enshrined into law. What we are doing here is extending those expenditure reductions and indeed deepening them.
With respect to small business, I think the best news for the small business sector is that there are no new taxes or no tax increases. I know that my hon. friend is disappointed about that because they are the party of high taxes, high spending and high deficits.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
What we have are a number of initiatives to assist small business. The Small Business Financing Program is extended. We have increased the maximum loan limits and changed the Small Businesses
April 27, 1993

Loans Act so it can be more effective. We have increased the labour-sponsored venture capital corporation credit, the UI premium relief for new jobs, new small business investment tax credit and assistance to the small oil companies which is really having a very positive effect. Indeed, there are steps to further reduce the compliance burden with respect to the GST. All of those things are very welcome in the small business community.

Mr. Speaker, if the minister really believes that, he has been away from the small business sector for far too long. The problem with his budget is that it does not just build on last December's statement, it builds on nine years of failure.
The minister talks about what the government is prepared to do for small business. The minister ought to know from his own background that the biggest problem small businesses face is the lack of capital. What is the government's response to lack of capital? Let me quote from this great document. The minister says: "We will explore ways to develop mechanisms to encourage investors," whatever that means. After countless studies and commissions, the Porter report, the prosperity initiative, that is a sentence riddled with cliches. Is exploring mechanisms the best thing this government can do to encourage small business?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that the small business federal tax rate is the lowest tax rate applied to small businesses in any country in the world. That in itself is a very important element.
We have the lowest interest rates in 20 years and the lowest inflation rate in 30 years. That is helpful. The Small Businesses Loans Act was indeed overhauled through an extensive consultation process. Indeed members opposite, his own colleagues, helped in that process. We got a good package, one the banks have responded to positively. For example, the Royal Bank, the Bank of Nova Scotia and the Toronto Dominion Bank have all responded very positively by providing extra premium rates for the Small Businesses Loans Act. They are also suggesting that more than $1 billion of new capital will flow to the small business sector in 1993 and that is good news.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Listening to the
Oral Questions
answers so far today, it is clear this is a pretty tired government in need of a period of long hibernation. The next election should provide that.
When it comes to the most serious economic issue facing Canadians, the job crisis, the government has chosen to do nothing but to accept 11 per cent unemployment this year and double digit unemployment next year. We see that one in four Canadians is unemployed, underemployed or has given up hope in this country. Hope is desperately needed.
Europe, Japan and the United States, major trading partners, have come out with jobs plans for their countries. In the case of Europe it is a jobs plan for countries of the European Community. This is a jobs plan for economic renewal.
Why is the government content in this budget to simply ride on the coat-tails of other governments? Why has the government not come out with a positive jobs plan that will give Canadians hope?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is in place right now an expenditure of $1.1 billion in this fiscal year and $1 billion plus in the next fiscal year to help bolster the economy from infrastructure to training and skills upgrading, to incentives for small business, to encouraging more trade and in particular to ensuring that the trade initiatives that have been so successful in creating more export demand are carried out and transformed into jobs.
I should advise the hon. member that since November employment growth has been growing at an annual rate of 2.8 per cent. That is higher than we had expected in this budget in which we predicted 1.7 per cent this year and 3 per cent next year.
I remind my hon. friend that we have had 200,000 new full-time jobs created since August, 48,000 new jobs last month and 26,000 new jobs in the manufacturing sector. There are clear signs of pick-up both in the manufacturing sector and in the export sector and hopefully soon in the domestic demand sector.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I remind the minister that the unemployment rate remains at 11 per cent. That is the official unemployment rate. The unofficial rate is

Oral Questions
much closer to about 19 per cent and youth unemployment is close to 20 per cent.
I say to the minister that he can stand in this House and say that his policies have created more jobs, but his policies have created more devastation in the last nine years in this country and we needed to see a budget to change that.
The government has addressed the issue of the deficit many times, although in this budget projection the deficit will not even decrease in the coming year. One of the major causes of deficit, in addition to the bad trade policies of this government, the high interest rate policy of this government and the GST, is high unemployment. Of course we have declining revenues with a declining number of people working.
Why does the government refuse to acknowledge that the deficit is simply a symptom of an economy that is not working? Why does it not recognize that for a country to work the people of that country must be working?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agreed that a healthy economy and lots of jobs is really the ultimate. That is what we are really trying to do.
We do have a recovery that has been slow in coming, but we have facilitated that recovery by the measures that we have taken. At the same time we have to deal with the deficit. We have tried to strike a balanced, responsible, realistic and achievable position, not to be bloodthirsty or Draconian, not to tackle the provinces, not to tackle senior citizens or veterans. We have attempted to adopt a responsible course of action, one that is achievable.
I can tell my hon. friend that I believe what we have laid out in the five-year program is achievable and will get us to a level of zero cash requirements at the end of the five-year period. Our deficit as a percentage of GDP will be .9 per cent. That is down from 5.1 per cent as it is today. We will have the lowest expenditures of government in more than 30 years at 13.9 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister. The projections of the minister for the future rival those of the psychics in The National Enquirer. Indeed, I think they have actually had better success with their predictions than the minister.

I have a question for the Minister. The government has made choices. It chose to ignore unemployment; it chose to attack programs which were important for ordinary people, such as subsidized housing, regional development, transportation subsidies, the CBC, and organizations assisting the underpriviledged. Instead, the government could have ended private family trust exemptions and deductions for business entertainment expenses.
Why does the government keep asking sacrifices from ordinary people rather than from the rich?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the finance minister looked at some of the Canadian headlines maybe he would get some idea of what people are really thinking.
Let us stop all this talk. Governing is a matter of choices. This government and this Minister of Finance had a choice. This government and this Minister of Finance chose to do nothing except to utter empty phrases and to accept unacceptable double digit levels of unemployment.
How can this government ignore the desperate need of Canadians for jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, governing is about choices and governing is about making difficult choices. In some cases we have to exercise restraint.
I must say that on every single solitary occasion we brought forward restraint measures to the House of Commons the Liberal Party voted against it and the NDP voted against it. So much for talking about the level of restraint.
Clearly a number of initiatives have been put in place as a result of the December statement. This budget builds on the December statement. It continues the expenditure reductions but it also continues the support in those particular areas of the economy that need strengthening. That is where the jobs are being created.
Oral Questions
That is why we are optimistic about achieving 7.5 per cent level in unemployment by 1997-98.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Yesterday in his budget he predicted a $32.6 billion deficit for the current year. That is up from previous predictions of $16.6 billion in 1991, $14 billion in 1990, and $15 billion in 1989. Furthermore, the minister's projection last year for the year just ended was off by a mere $8 billion.
In a budget devoid of strategy for economic growth and new jobs, how can the minister expect Canadians to take seriously the deficit projections he has put in this year's budget?

The hon. member knows very well that because of the recession and the global economic slowdown we have had a shortfall in revenues of some $9 billion in 1992-1993. We project that similar shortfalls in revenues will be expected in the other years as well.
What we have done here is we have constrained expenditures. As a matter of fact we have brought them down by about $900 billion from where we originally were. We are exercising prudence and restraint on the expenditure side. What we are doing is trying to bolster economic growth-

assumptions aside would agree, has some pretty optimistic growth forecasts in it. It projects a deficit of $8 billion five years from now.

That is not good enough for us. Zero cash requirements is what we are after. A .9 per cent deficit to GDP ratio is what we are after and the lowest level of government expenditure in 30 years. That is what we are after and that is what our objectives will achieve.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Most independent agencies forecast unemployment at greater than 10 per cent for the decade and growth at around 2.5 per cent. The wizard of finance conjures growth at 4.25 per cent and unemployment at 7.6 per cent by 1997-1998.

My question is as follows: would it not be reasonable for the 1.5 million unemployed to conclude they are out of work because this government does not know what it is talking about and it does not know what it is doing?

When we look around the world in terms of the global economy, we see Japan's growth at 1.3 per cent, Germany at minus 1.3 per cent, Italy at .3 per cent and the U.K. at 1.4 per cent. We are a part of the global economy. There is no question about that.
The hon. member says my figures and my forecast are unrealistic. The objective analysts from New York suggest-
In the Village Voice.

speechtext: -again that the budget is delivering the fruits of structural change in public financing undertaken in recent years and which were not harvested because of the prolonged recession. Mr. Speaker, yesterday's announcement of major cuts to regional development has resulted in the unjustified cancellation of the Forest Development Agreement funding which is a major factor in Canada's goal to attain sustainable forest development.
This irresponsible Conservative government does not realize the impact that this cancellation will have on rural Canada and much more to the forest industry which cannot absorb those cuts. this sector further they will certainly have the opportunity to do so.

Canso): Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Finance.

because we recognize the difficult circumstances that many of the provinces are in.

I want to ask the Minister of Finance why this government is unilaterally withdrawing its responsibility to provide funds for social housing. Does he not realize that good housing policy is good social policy and is good economic policy for this country?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we have in front of us is a budget, as I was saying this morning, which has done absolutely nothing to increase jobs in this country. It contains no initiatives to give us new direction for the unemployed.
I see the Minister of Finance being congratulated by his colleagues. It can only be for having succeeded in putting in 94 pages not a single solitary new thought and for wasting hundreds of thousands of trees in the process. I suspect the colleagues congratulating him must come from forestry regions of the country.
What is so tragic about this budget is not just what is not there but what could have been there. We could have had moves to start to make our tax system fair by closing some of the loopholes at the top, loopholes like those the Auditor General identified last year that let large corporations take over $1 billion out of Canada tax-free, which we the taxpayers of the country have to make up.
We could have had initiatives to take action to make the GST gradually disappear so as to help small business and to help consumers across Canada. We could have had moves to put into effect a minimum corporate tax so that we got away from the scandal of large scale corporations being completely free of corporate tax even when they have made profits in Canada.
We could have had those initiatives. We could have had initiatives to see to it that in this country as in 22 of the other OECD countries the fortunes of people who are wealthy when they die and pass them on to their children and their friends are taxed and make a contribution to making our society better.
We could have taken that money and used it to get people back to work. We could have had initiatives on child care, the establishment of a national child care program such as the Prime Minister has promised for so many years and has failed to provide. We could have had an infrastructure program to give us some real sense of building a base for our economy for the future, a national investment fund to help the small scale and medium sized businesses in Canada that so badly need venture capital. We could in short have had a national jobs plan to put 1.5 million Canadians back to work, to bring the unemployment rate down and to put Canadians in positions where they are contributing to our tax rates instead of taking from our budgets.
Let me conclude by moving the following amendment to the amendment that has been moved:
That the following words be added after the words "economic recovery":
"by way of a national child care program, an infrastructure
program, a national investment fund, and a national jobs plan".
If we took this direction we would put Canada back to work. We would give Canadians hope. We would give our country a future built not on smoke and mirrors, not on Alice in Wonderland projections, but on solid economic ideas to give us a real basis for jobs in all of this country.
That is the direction in which we have to move. I hope it is the direction in this next election that people in Canada choose to take.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could ask my friend a question about his speech on the budget.
In his speech on page 3 of the budget booklet the Minister of Finance made the following statement:
Less borrowing, lower taxes, more jobs and more choice: that is the direction in which people want to go. And that is the direction in which this government is going.
April 27, 1993

Does he agree that this statement is completely false having regard to the fact that the government is borrowing both here and abroad at record levels, that taxes have increased 30-some times since the government took office and in fact now as a percentage of GNP has reached over 39 per cent from a level of about 33.8 per cent when the government took office in 1984, that fewer jobs are available in Canada because our unemployment rate has gone up, not down, and that Canadians are getting less and less choice because of the cutbacks in government programs? Would he not agree that this statement made by the minister is completely false and misleading?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly the statement set out in the speech, as is so much in the speech, is a wild exaggeration in terms of the government's achievements.
To suggest the government is achieving less borrowing when in fact its borrowing has increased is simply wrong. To suggest that it is establishing lowering taxes is wrong. This is the government that put the GST into effect.
These are the parents of the GST across the aisle. Every Conservative who marches out to seek votes in this election should carry with him and her a little sign saying "I am responsible for the GST," just to remind people that is where it comes from.
Turning to more jobs, there have been more jobs for Conservative patronage appointees. There have been more jobs in the Senate for friends of the Prime Minister. There have not been more jobs for Canadians.
They promised 550,000 jobs from free trade. What they have given us is a loss of over 400,000 jobs in manufacturing and an unemployment rate of 11 per cent as of the most recent month compared to an unemployment rate of around 7.5 per cent when the free trade deal came into effect.
Dealing with more choice, this government believes that if it gives things to the market we will automatically get more choice. What Canadians have discovered is that by giving things to the marketplace to rule they do not get more choice; they get less choice.
The Budget
I have just one small example. Let us lookback to 1988 when this government was re-elected and think of the airline industry at that stage. There were four national airlines. We had Wardair operating scheduled services across the country. We had PWA operating scheduled services throughout the country. We had Air Canada. We had Canadian Pacific.
This government said: "Let's deregulate. Let's add even more choice." For a little while we had all sorts of little regional carriers throw themselves up into the air. Very soon they crashed to the ground and were taken over by other companies. We now have just two airlines: Air Canada and Canadian, and both of them are sick. We are not getting more choice. We are getting less choice as a consequence of the ideology rather than the thinking this government follows.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
could save at least $10 billion if we eliminated this duplication between the provinces and the federal government. We could have saved $10 billion per year right there.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think everyone will agree that my colleague, the Minister of Finance, tabled a responsible and decisive budget.
The fiscal plan set out in the budget builds on the action taken last December, by extending and deepening
the expenditure reductions. While recent fiscal pressures have resulted from revenue shortfalls, the solution is not to raise revenues. It is to learn to live within our means.
With this action, the deficit target for 1993-94 will be met and there will be no new borrowings by the end of the fiscal planning period. Achieving these fiscal objectives is key to sustained economic expansion and the job and income gains that will come with it.
My remarks will provide additional context and detail on the measures announced in the budget, particularly the reductions in the cost of government. This action will over time have a major effect on the operations of government and the management of the Public Service.
These measures, together with the reductions announced in the economic and fiscal statement tabled in this House last December, will yield expenditure savings of $7.5 billion in government operations over the next five years. This is a major contribution to the total debt reduction effort of $30 billion. These cuts build on this government's ongoing commitment and actions to reduce operating costs and increase effeciency in government.

As set out in the budget, operating budgets and reserves for contingencies and new initiatives were reduced by $300 million in 1993-94, rising to $1.2 billion by 1997-98. This means that for the last four years of the fiscal framework the operating reserve is being reduced by 50 per cent from an already tight level.
Last December non-defence operating budgets were reduced by $1 billion in 1993-94 and by $1.7 billion in 1994-95. Taking into account the budget measures announced yesterday, the typical manager will in effect face an operating budget reduction of 3 per cent in 1993-94 and 5 per cent in 1994-5, reaching 10 per cent by 1997-98.
The reduction in most grant and contribution programs to organizations and interest groups announced last December will be extended and deepened to 15 per cent in 1995-96 and to 20 per cent in future years. These reductions will be implemented in a prudent and reasonable manner reflecting government priorities.


April 27, 1993

We recognize that given the magnitude of the reduction a fundamental review of a number of existing programs will be required. Scarce resources will have to be devoted to funding the highest priority programs.

The Minister of Finance also announced a number of other reductions across government: regional funding, the green plan, granting councils, international assistance, defence, social housing, the CBC and VIA Rail. We are far from being alone in a financial crunch. Most countries are facing tough economic and fiscal situations and most are responding to the large revenue shortfalls by taking similar action to reduce expenditures.
Closer to home we have only to look at the recent provincial budgets and statements. These reinforce the harsh reality that restraint is not just the order of the day, but of years to come. In the earlier years, we used restraint in large part to cut the fat that had accumulated from years of steady growth in government expenditures. As time passed, departments and agencies have had to find more innovative ways to deliver programs and services. They have had no choice to undertake productivity-increasing investments, and to make better use of their shrinking resources.
The demand for services increases with population and so do workload. Departments and agencies are pressed even more vigorously to re-engineer their administrative overhead and to deliver services at lower costs. Resources are having to be redirected to the point of service for the client and away from overhead and administrative processes.
Departments have no choice but to seize every opportunity for efficiency gains from investments in training and development and in information technology. This by itself is not enough, however, as we no longer have the means to pay for all the current programs, even less to tolerate duplication of services and other inefficiencies.

These latest measures will necessitate taking a hard look at priorities and making some difficult choices indeed. As I said in my speech during the debate on the December economic and fiscal statement, it will simply not be possible to do more with less.
The Budget
In some instances activities will be reduced and points of service delivery closed. As an example, there are currently 64 Canada immigration centres. These points of service are being reduced to 51, of which 22 will be co-located in Canada employment centres. External Affairs is closing nine missions including three embassies. It will also mean getting out of some lines of business.
Reducing the funds available for government operations will have an effect on employment in the Public Service. Currently salaries account for roughly 55 per cent of operating budgets. Assuming this proportion is maintained in coming years, we can expect that the reduction in total employment resulting from this budget will be approximately 16,500 by 1995-98. Indeed, based on past experience, the number of people affected will be significantly higher once the impacts of changing program priorities, service delivery innovations, new information technology and organizational adjustment are taken into account and as the mix of skills and people within a department and across departments continues to change over time.
In the period from 1985 to 1990, while the net reduction in employment was 10,700 it is estimated that approximately twice this number of positions were eliminated while new positions in other program areas were created.
A substantial portion of the anticipated reduction in total employment of 16,500 can be handled through retirements and resignations. We must not forget that some 9,000 employees leave the Public Service each year. However it is not realistic to assume that we will be able to manage all personnel reductions through attrition.
Most of the government's administrative and program operations are being redesigned to increase efficiency and the resultant changes will inevitably produce an imbalance between the skills needed and the skills available in a particular location. This is not unique to this government. It is much the same in the private sector and in the other levels of government.
As a practical matter employment in the federal public sector actually increased in 1992 by about 1,000 to a little more than 235,000 people. This reflects a wide range of increases and decreases across departments and agen-

April 27, 1993
The Budget
cies. Five departments and agencies showed employment increases of 300 or more in 1992, specifically Employment and Immigration Canada, Revenue Canada Customs and Excise, Correctional Services Canada, Health and Welfare Canada and Agriculture Canada. Four departments showed a decline of 300 or more: National Defence, Revenue Canada Taxation, Transport Canada and Statistics Canada.
In areas where there were reductions the persons affected did not necessarily have the skills needed in departments that were growing or these employees were not able to take advantage of these new demands because of their location.
The numbers are only part of the story. I do want to emphasize that the underlying purpose of the action we are taking is to secure savings in government expenditure. It is not to reduce the work force.
In the world of the 1990s the government needs employment policies that promote a flexible and more adaptive federal work force. Existing policies, including the work force adjustment directive, must be reviewed. There are aspects of the directive that we can no longer afford in the present economic climate. There are others which severely restrict our ability to modify the shape and size of the work force.
Therefore the government will seek some basic changes to the directive to give managers added flexibility. We will continue to fulfil our responsibilities as a fair employer but we must do so in the context of the economic and fiscal realities of the 1990s. We will invite unions to work with us toward realistic arrangements during negotiations beginning this summer as part of the regular triennial review.
We believe that public servants understand the economic realities faced by the government. I do believe that they understand these realities. I am convinced that they and their unions will want to work with us in finding innovative solutions to the problems we are facing. We are currently consulting with departments on this and are not ready to set out our proposals. Clearly we will be seeking significant changes.

As I see it, adaptability and innovation in the Public Service is key to its long-term effectiveness. This means that the institution as a whole, its organizational units, its management and every one of its employees must be able to adapt quickly to change. We must also continually strive to find better ways to deliver government services more efficiently.
One approach is to use information technology in new ways to improve administrative and program delivery processes. Information technology allows us to provide services to clients at lower overall costs to the government and, in many cases, to the clients.
The government is aggressively pursuing electronic means for conducting many of its routine transactions. This strategy also hinges on the use of electronic data interchange or EDI and complementary technologies such as bar coding.
Over 20 EDI initiatives are now under way, including electronic documentation at ports of entry, collection of remittances for GST and source deductions, electronic filing of GST and personal income taxes, and many, many others.
I am proud the federal government is becoming a leader in implementing EDI in Canada. Indeed I am pleased to note that on June 30, Supply and Services Canada's new electronic initiative FASTRACK will begin directly linking suppliers electronically with federal departments and agencies. This use of EDI for the procurement of goods and services and, in future, for related payments will mean lower costs for the government and for its suppliers. It will also contribute to an EDI-capable business sector, enabling it to better compete in the global economy.
We are innovating in other ways. We have established 12 special operating agencies and four more are on the way: Indian Oil and Gas Canada; the Transport Canada Training Institute; Translation Services; and Surveys and Mapping. The last three were announced in this Budget. They are service oriented operations given added flexibility to apply the best management practices in order to improve service delivery. Many Canadians have seen the improved service provided by the Passport Office, an early special operating agency.
April 27, 1993

The Budget
Across Canada, 129 InfoCentres have opened in Canada Employment Centres to provide Canadians with basic information on government services to more conveniently. Twelve departments are working together to make services available to the public through common government, rather than departmental, access points.
Through these InfoCentres clients can receive basic information on more than 50 of the most commonly used government programs like pensions, training and unemployment insurance, and bidding on government cheques replaced. They have access to hot-line services to departments when they require answers to more complex questions. Facilities are also made available for clients to meet with departments on specific matters-income tax advice for example.
We are also changing how we provide services to the business client who is confronted by a bewildering array of federal, provincial, municipal and private sector services.
The Canada Business Service Centres (CBSCs) are one among several initiatives. There are currently three CBSCs in operation, in Edmonton, Winnipeg and Halifax, which provide the business community with quick and accurate referrals to government services, programs and information at a single point of service. They are serving as the pilot for a network of single-windows that will soon extend from coast to coast. Discussions have begun on three others and it is our intention to establish a CBSC in at least one major urban centre in each province.
In Edmonton, the CBSC is a shared walk-in centre operated through a partnership of 15 federal departments and agencies.

To conclude, I was pleased to see that the premier of Alberta announced last week in the legislative assembly that his government intended to reform the regulatory system. I congratulate him and offer my support to any of the other provinces that choose to launch their own regulatory reviews. They can count on the co-operation and support of my colleagues and myself. We are eager to share the experience we have gained in our own milieu and we will provide whatever assistance possible should the provinces decide to move forward in this area.

In conclusion, I recognize the contribution that public servants have made and will continue to make, as we grapple with these difficult issues at a time of sweeping changes in government operations. Public servants are not afraid of these changes.
Unlike our hon. friends opposite, they are not afraid. These are people who deal with the public. They-and I address this to Public Service employees at all levels of government-must forge a strong sense of common purpose that they are all serving one taxpaying public, and that their well-being is inextricably linked to that of this public. This goes for us politicians too.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister a question about the information centres the government has established so that people can inquire about all the various services it provides.

In my constituency of Kingston and the Islands it has set up one of these places. Seniors have to walk to it because it will not take telephone calls there and it does not give out its telephone number. Seniors have to telephone Ottawa on a 1-800 number, which is busy whenever they call. People wait 30, 40, or 50 minutes, they dial and dial and cannot get through because this line is tied up all the time. When they do they get a different person every time they call and have to provide different information. There is no continuity and there is no co-ordination. People are very angry at the lack of service.
The minister tries to pretend this is all just rosy and that everything is improving. It is not. It is getting worse. In his budget yesterday the Minister of Finance talked about Canadians having more choice with this government. They are getting less choice. They are getting poorer service. They are getting rotten service from this government because of its constant closure and shift to these so-called more efficient systems. This is not more efficient. This is costing Canadian taxpayers a lot of money because they have to make all these telephone calls and repeat themselves time after time when they phone because the person they are dealing with is never the same.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
It is a hopeless system. The minister must know it. Why does he not abandon this? It is fine to lump them all together. That may make sense, but then make the office accessible to the public and not on some distant bus route so that people who have difficulty getting out and about are forced into phoning Ottawa or Toronto in order to get information.
It is a ridiculous system. The minister must know it. For him to stand with a straight face and tell us that everything is just great stretches all belief. I can see why he switches languages. He would want to say it in another language so that some of us cannot follow the logic because there is no logic to it.
I would appreciate the minister clarifying this for us. [Translation]

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands also tried to throw me by switching from French to English, but I think I understood what he meant.
I want to tell him that the experience I have had with information centres is quite extraordinary. You may have heard of a successful initiative in Quebec called Commu-nication-Quebec, for which I was responsible. I dismantled a highly centralized service and established centres in the various regions so that citizens could have support in their dealings with the government. That is similar to what we have been trying to do with federal organizations. In every area, we noticed a proliferation of organizations, representatives, departments, bits of departments and a lack of means. We obviously do not have the means to provide complete services to residents from every region of this country. That is impossible. We need to ensure that the information is stored somewhere and that there is a centre where people can get support when they deal with the government.
Many such centres in Canada are very successful. We are working with Communication-Quebec and other provincial governments and I am sure these centres will get better. I am not saying there are no errors and no problems, but the alternative to these centres is nothing at all.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two short questions.
The minister talked about reductions in staff. He did not mention reductions in service. Neither did he mention the increase in the use of outside contractors to do the work.
I wonder if the minister has had any studies done or has done any which he could share with us showing that the use of outside contractors has actually saved the government money for the same level of service.
I have another question. Among the departments he mentioned where staff reductions have been considerable was Revenue Canada. Year after year I have heard the Auditor General say that if the department had hired more auditors each one of them would bring in perhaps 10 times as much revenue as it would cost for that employee. I wonder if it is cost effective to reduce the staff in Revenue Canada as much as has been done.
The last Auditor General's report said that some $500 million to $600 million of revenue is being lost because corporations are moving their incomes out of this jurisdiction into others that are more favourable to them. With auditors Revenue Canada would we be able to capture some or all of that $500 million to $600 million?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are not proceeding with staff reduction because we want to reduce staff per se. We are just looking for ways to make the delivery of service as efficient and as inexpensive as possible.
I am sure that the hon. member is aware that as of April 1 this year we changed our administrative system to operating budgets. Each department is given an over-all operating budget within which they can move their resources around to get the best mix to deliver services.
Sometimes I have the feeling that the hon. member or the people across the aisle believe that the purpose of the Public Service is to be a big employment agency. We are not here to hire people. We are here to deliver services with people. If we can find a way of doing it better at a lower cost then I do not see what on earth should prevent us from doing it.
I think civil servants understand this. I am convinced that the number of reductions over the coming years will be very light compared to the size of this government's operation, which is close to a quarter of a million employees. Compared to any organization in Canada of a small, medium or large size that has had to get rid of hundreds of thousands of people, we have been very
April 27, 1993

attentive to our work force and have been very protective and we intend to continue to do this.
However the purpose of government services is not to find jobs for people, it is to deliver service professionally, efficiently, with the best possible people and at the lowest possible cost.
If there is a way of doing it with fewer people why should we not do it if we can save money? Why should we spend money just for the pleasure of repeating these mistakes of the past?
As for contracting out, yes, we can contract out when we find that it is a more efficient way of doing things for short-term action or areas in which we do not want to be involved forever. It could be snow removal or things of that sort which occur at certain periods of the year. We cannot have permanent staff just waiting there for winter to arrive so we use the private sector. They compete against each other and in this way we can lower our costs. We recruit excellent, well trained managers. We train them when the need occurs and they are asked to provide the services. They are given a budget and they must account for it. They have to devise ways of trying to do as much and more if possible with as little money as we can give them.
Basically this is the philosophy. It is not a religious approach. It is just a practical approach that Canadians expect from us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I see that I have to be very brief.
This budget has repeated promises to reduce the debt and deficit the same way the government has done for nine years. We all know that this has not resulted in a reduction but in an increase in the debt and deficit.
I wonder if the President of the Treasury Board has paid any attention whatsoever to the report of the Conference Board of Canada that commented on the December 2 financial statement. It said that the over-all impact of the measures of the government will be contradictory and will lower the real GDP rate by roughly 0.1 per cent-that is in fact 10 per cent of the expected GDP increase-and by 2 per cent in 1993. It promises that the dampening effect on economic recovery would be even greater if the provinces followed the
The Budget
federal government's example of restraining public sector wages and employment. Does he realize the impact of the decisions of this budget on economic recovery?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish the hon. member would help me reconcile this with the statement of the House leader today in this House who blamed us for not cutting enough and reducing our expenditure enough.
This is the problem that I would like her to address. Who should I believe? Do I take into account her remarks or the remarks of the hon. Liberal House leader? He told us that we have been trying to tackle our expenditure and deficit and that we have not been successful. Each time we cut $1 million it was opposed.
We have been trying and we have been successful. We have brought the deficit down compared with the GDP, which is very important. It is half of what it was. It is not enough and we want to do more. We had a statement in December. There was some slippage. We are taking corrective action. We will continue to fight. It is very difficult to do but we are not going to abandon it.
Our commitment is to put this fiscal House in order. We do understand that we have to keep a balance. If we had taken more out of the economy at this stage-we have taken $3.8 billion from the coming year-it would have had a greater impact.
I think the Liberals should make up their minds which way they want it.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of my constituents in this House of Commons, especially on this occasion when I am given the opportunity to speak to what is not only a pre-election budget but also this government's last budget. I know that Canadians rejoice that they will not have to deal with this particular government much longer.
I wondered when I sat in this House yesterday, why we went through this exercise. There were so many balloons floated up before the budget came out. All of a sudden the budget came and there was really nothing in it. If one wanted to speak to the budget at all one could only deal with the impact of this particular statement or budget on this particular year because obviously there will be a new

April 27, 1993
The Budget
leader within 60 days. There will be an election and there will be a new government with very many different faces sitting in this House of Commons. All we can talk about is the first portion. The rest is all conjecture and whatever nice things they want to say.
Let us look at what happens in this budget for 1993-94. The government is saying that it is going to cut things to the tune of I believe $3.8 billion. Let me remind Canadians that in December's economic statement it was cutting by $2.8 billion. Therefore it has only found approximately $1 billion. Of that $1 billion one of the savings, so to speak, is going to be some $625 million in GST refund cheques. It is not really saving that money. It is just not going to give out refunds in January 1994. It is going to wait until the end of its fiscal year, which is March 31, 1994. One will get one's cheque on April 1. In that way on the government's books it can show a decrease in what it is paying out on GST rebates of more than $600 million for the years 1993 and 1994.
There is not really a lot in this budget for 1993-94 in terms of cutting. That leaves maybe another $250 million or $300 million that is going to be cut from a number of other areas such as advocacy groups. The list goes on. I am just wondering why.
Prior to the budget coming out I happened to read an article in The Ottawa Citizen of April 20, 1993 written by Mr. Don McGillivray: "Usually a budget represents the dollars and cents form of a government's agreed policy. This time it is being presented when the governing party does not know who its leader will be in 60 days or who that leader will choose as finance minister or what will be the economic policies of the new minister and future finance minister. In other words, a budget now is a lame duck document, an interim financial statement from an outgoing administration. Mazankowski, since he is in temporary possession of the taxpayers' cash, has the power to issue political pamphlets at public expense."
Is that really the only reason that we have this budget at this time? Is it so that this particular government, at taxpayers' expense, can go out and boast and brag about all of the things that will happen when it is not there any more? As a matter of fact, some of them will happen after a second election.
One realizes there is going to be an election this year. There has to be one. Other projections go as far as five and six years from now. There could be many elections between now and then. I find it very strange to hear those members boasting about how they will cut the deficit by $30 billion and how they will reduce the debt in four or five years.
It is all really a game. I do not believe that Canadians appreciate being used in that fashion. I wonder at the mentality that carries this on because it has built Canadians up to expect some massive cuts. Did it believe that when it did not have the massive cuts that all Canadians would celebrate and vote Conservative next time around? I do not think the government gives much credit for intelligence. It is high time it considers it. On the other hand we do not have to worry about it because it will be gone after the next time.
Before the minister brought in his budget he spoke proudly of the fact that Canadians will get what they want. He clearly stated yesterday that there will be no new taxes or tax increases. Obviously we cannot afford more increases. We have already been taxed to death. This is the government that raised taxes of all kinds at least 35 times in the last 9 years.
As the Liberal leader stated, the tired old Conservative government is obviously showing more concern for its re-election plan than for the welfare of the Canadian people. It is clear that this government is committed to a jobless recovery.
The phrase jobless recovery comes from the The Work of Nations that is a book written by Robert Reich while he was still at Harvard. By the way this Mr. Reich is the Secretary of Labour for President Clinton. Reich took the American context to apply this term.
However unfortunately for Canadians the Tories have transplanted the reality of a jobless recovery onto the Canadian scene. That means that yes, we do produce more goods. Some corporations may make larger profits but it all has to do with increased productivity and no new jobs. That is where the term jobless recovery comes into the picture.
Canadians want to work and they want recovery but they also want good paying jobs. Right now they are underemployed and unemployed by the hundreds of thousands. As a matter of fact we have a figure of unemployment but that does not bring into consideration
April 27, 1993

the large number of people who work at part time jobs and short term contract jobs. It is especially crucial for our younger generation made up of those young people who are now in their twenties and have graduated from university and who are out there looking for work. It is especially frustrating for them.
It leads me to believe that this government has almost decided to write off this generation. We cannot afford to do that with the brilliant minds of our young people and the skills that some of them do possess.
Unless Canada rebuilds the infrastructure that serves its industries and more importantly that provides and improves the skills of its workers, then economic recovery may generate few new jobs. There is absolutely nothing in this budget that will get the economy moving again and put Canadians back to work.
The government is telling Canadians: "Yes, we are coming out of the recession and therefore our economy will be recovering." However it fails to recognize that the economy is undergoing a fundamental restructuring. The government has no detailed economic plan to nurture innovation, training and infrastructure that are the building blocks of a strong and prosperous economy.
Not too long ago Statistics Canada announced that the recession was over. It along with the Conservative think-tanks based their optimism on a selective set of statistics: rising exports, falling interest rates, continuing low inflation and a decline in the rate of personal and business bankruptcies.
Facts and figures that do not fit this cheerful scenario are ignored. I am referring to the still surging tide of lay-offs, the growing number of poor and homeless, the lengthening line-ups at food banks and welfare offices. We are in a state of social distress.
Bankers and business executives say that what counts is the upturn in profits. Prosperity is measured in corporate balance sheets, not in job creation.
Governments have seen to it that in both the public and private sector job cuts and more job cuts are necessary for Canada to become competitive. They tell us monthly that it is part of an economic restructuring process.
The Budget
Restructuring is the current buzz word in business and government, but what does it really mean? The dictionary definition is "to replace one structure with another." I would like to know where the new economic structure is for Canada. Can we see the old economy being torn down while we look in vain for its substitute? If it exists even in the planning stages, it certainly is not discernible. Neither are the new jobs that the victims of restructuring so desperately need. We do not know where they are coming from.
One of the tragic downfalls or victims of these policies is of course our young people. Generation x is the contemporary way to describe the lost generation, the followers of the baby-boomers. Young people today and generations x, y and z to follow will find it difficult to get jobs of any kind.
This is this year; I am not talking about the future. Young people cannot find jobs now. Many of them graduated from university this year. Many graduated two years ago and are out there in the job market. Many of them are looking for summer work to pay for their studies. Where are they going to get this help? Certainly not from the Conservative government across the way.
I can speak on this because I have children in that age group. Their friends and all of the people I know in their age groups have a very difficult time getting jobs. They are smart, and like to work. They want to work and are well educated. It is a crime to see them not being able to use their skills.
I want to talk about the deficit. It is fine to speak of dealing with the deficit. Let us face it. This government has made it a religion to talk about deficit cutting and debt cutting.
In 1984 the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre, said he had a plan. He warned that if this plan was not implemented net public debt would more than double from its level then rising to over $400 billion by the early 1990s. Imagine how terrible it would have been had we only been at $400 billion for the debt. We are at $450 billion. That is how well this government has looked after this religion of deficit and debt. After nine years they are higher than what was predicted.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
In 1985 the then Minister of Finance again said that he was in control. He said it over and over. In fact he was so confident that he subtitled his May 23, 1985 budget speech "Securing Economic Renewal" and told Canadians how he was going to reduce the debt and deficit. This is what he said: "I am implementing a clear and realistic medium-term plan to control our debt. We have put in place a plan that will meet the need for sustained reduction of deficits over the medium term. We have acted to control and reduce deficits in a balanced and careful way that will not tip the economy off its course of growth."
The result was not good. It was a shrinking economy, massive unemployment and line-ups at food banks and the UIC offices. It was what the Conference Board called a made-in-Canada recession.
As recently as the Februaiy 1990 budget, the Tories told us that the $30.5 billion would be reduced to $14 billion by 1993. It is now 1993 and the deficit has been clocked at $34.4 billion. Of course now we have been told that it will be $35.5 billion. It continues to be far more than what they have said it would be.
Now the Minister of National Defence says she is going to eliminate the federal deficit within five years. The Minister of the Environment says he can do it in four. But they do not say how because they know it cannot be done without radical cuts to social programs and transfer payments.
Even then we do not know that economic growth would follow. Even the Minister of Finance knows it cannot be done as quickly as what they are saying. He said that if the whole government operation were shut down it would not balance the deficit. We would save $15 billion or $16 billion and the senior citizens and the veterans of this great country would not be receiving their cheques. This was in an interview on CBC Prime Time News in December 1992.
Maybe that is why none of the Tory candidates are talking specifics when it comes to investing in people or helping Canadian firms to get ready for NAFTA. They do not understand that any successful battle against the debt and deficit will require not only expenditure cuts but also a thoughtful plan for economic growth. Only then would we put Canadians back to work and generate the additional revenues to put Canada's fiscal house in order.
I said today in Question Period that governing is about choices. This government is the one in the driver's seat and it makes the choices. It has chosen to do nothing. It has chosen to ignore Canadians and their need for real hope. If hope is not given to Canadians, even those who have jobs fear they will lose them. They hold back and do not buy the things that perhaps they would if they had a little bit of hope and faith in the future.
We then fall into the vicious cycle of restraint and depression. Sales go down. There are bankruptcies and people get laid off. It continues on and on. It would have been a great gift to Canadians if after these terrible nine years of government it had at least tried once during that time to do something for the average Canadian.
The government should have tried to do something for those Canadians who are crying for hope and who want to work. Canadians are hard working and they like to have this independence. They want to share in the wealth of this country. It cannot be done when they are without work and without hope. Young people need a chance to build a life for themselves so that they also can pass on the benefits to their children in the future.
We know any government that takes over will have to deal with the deficit. There is no doubt that we all will. It is not whether we will or we will not deal with the deficit; it is how we will do it. We will do it by redefining government, by refocusing the powers of government to serve the people of Canada. We will not do it by spending more, but by reallocating government priorities.
Canadians know this and we know Canadians are worth while. The more they work, the better it is for this economy. The better it is for this economy, the better the regions of Canada will fare and the more able they will be to contribute to the wealth of this country. All that they ask is to be given half a chance.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Marc Robitaille (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to my colleague who mentioned in her speech that Canadians were expecting massive cuts. From what the hon. member said at the beginning of her speech, you would believe that no major cuts were announced yesterday. Yet, during Question Period, her Liberal colleagues spent an hour accusing
April 27, 1993

the Minister of Finance of having made monstrous cuts. They cannot constantly speak from both sides of their mouth. They have to make up their minds in the end: either there were cuts or there were not. Today the hon. member is saying that there were no major cuts and that we did nothing to reduce the deficit, but her own colleagues said the opposite for an hour during question period.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member also mentioned that these policies hurt young people, but the fact of the matter is that they are actually victims of Liberal policies. It is the Liberal Party that let government finances get out of hand, which in turn compromised the future of young Canadians. That is what they are victims of. They are victims of this accumulated debt, while we are trying to be fair and equitable. It goes like this: "We want to have a good time. So what if we get into debt. Let the next generation pay." That is what the young could be victims of if we do not act immediately.
Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member that every budget reduction measure taken by this government over the past nine years has been systematically opposed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is a speech!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not a speech, just comments I am making as part of this period for questions and comments. Wake up! Thke the time to come in, then you will know what to talk about.
A few days ago, we heard how the leader of the Liberal Party would solve the deficit problem. He would bring the deficit down to 3 per cent of gross domestic product. I would like to remind the House-and I am getting to my question-that in 1984, when this government came to power, the deficit as a proportion of GDP was 8.5 per cent, but it is now down to 5.5 per cent. I think this is not a solution in itself but rather an objective.
I am getting to my question. The hon. member is right, some of our predictions were off the mark. Bear in mind however that these previous budget forecasts were off the mark because revenues were down, not because expenditure controls were not fully adhered to.
The Budget
In this budget, and this is my question, policies to assist small and medium-sized businesses are pursued to create jobs, research and development assistance is maintained and there are no tax increases. Are the hon. member and her party prepared to support a budget that will continue to provide assistance to the small business sector for job creation, without increasing taxes?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to respond to one of the statements made by the hon. member. He said that Canadians wanted to treat themselves. I can tell you that the Conservatives have been treating themselves and their friends for nine years. They loved those nine years. The prime minister is still treating himself today to a trip around the world. Why? Maybe he is looking for a job, I do not know but he tells Canadians to tighten their belts. It is okay for them but not for him. He has to go and play the big shot around the world because his mandate is coming to an end. Nobody can tell him what to do any more.
Small business owners cannot afford such a trip around the world.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Answer the questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Small business owners have big problems with taxes imposed by this government. I know the Tories have not raised taxes this time, but have they not done enough to destroy those small businesses? Tell me, it is impossible-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: She is not answering the questions.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I would ask the hon. member not to distract the Speaker who is listening carefully and I would ask the hon. member for Sudbury to conclude her remarks.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext:
