subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before commenting on the new budget brought down by the Minister of Finance, I would like to say that I have agreed to share my speaking time with another member of the Conservative caucus.
Since 19841 have attended nine budget speeches, eight by Mr. Wilson and the last two by Mr. Mazankowski.
As soon as debate started on the budget, opposition parties would rise to say they were either unhappy about tax increases, because there were some tax increases initially, or about spending cuts. That is what they would say, and later on, when they had to vote on the budget, they always voted against spending cuts and tax increases of any kind.
There were also the reactions of Canadians to these speeches. Some groups felt they were penalized by specific measures in the budget which had a negative impact on them. Other groups said the government was not doing enough to cut spending, at a time when they felt spending cuts in departments should be accelerated. The government kept on gradually cutting back spending and has now stopped raising taxes.
April 27, 1993

The results in the medium term, and I am not referring to the budget's impact in the media the day after the budget speech, have been such that editorial writers, economists, entrepreneurs, business people and consumers appreciated how our economy has developed and prospered in the process.
During the past 12 months, four major provincial governments brought down their budgets and made certain economic decisions. The most obvious example is the socialist government in Ontario, which now supports spending cuts and is against big tax increases. This is a first, but it is also the first time this party has been in power.
We also have a socialist government in British Columbia. The party's philosophy has been to spend money they do not have. Here again, the party finally realized it was time to live within one's means, and its budget contained more restrictions on spending and tax increases.
We saw the same phenomenon in Saskatchewan, where the country's third socialist government has cut spending and does not intend to introduce undue tax increases. Premier Bob Rae of Ontario told party supporters-the groups that elected him and Ontario's major unions-in order to justify the position he was about to take on major budget cutbacks: we have to be careful, and maybe it would be nice to get some guidelines from the International Monetary Fund. The Premier of Ontario is prepared to abandon the concept of running a government independently by saying they would welcome a statement by the International Monetary Fund that they should apply further restrictions to government spending in Ontario. That is an important point.
We in the Conservative government did not wait for instructions from international organizations. We adopted measures that prevented foreign lenders from calling the loans because we Canadians have a foreign debt of $275 billion to $300 billion. If we did not adopt restricted measures, interest rates would go up, the dollar would go down and inflation would increase. We would have the same problems we had in 1984, after the Liberals lost the election.
Today, our policy is to control spending constantly instead of making a sudden break with the past, which
The Budget
would have been disastrous for the economy. We have always preferred to reduce spending and control tax increases. What has been the impact of this policy so far? The best news is that in every Canadian family, in every household, every single taxpayer is paying interest rates of 5 to 6 or 6.5 per cent. Today people are not experiencing a reduction in the purchasing power of their dollar, as was the case when we had 12 to 14 per cent inflation in 1982. Today inflation is around 1.5 per cent.
The Canadian dollar enjoys respect throughout the world, and that is why every Thursday, when $8 billion changes hands, lenders still have confidence in the Canadian dollar and interest rates are gradually going down.
That is also the message we were given yesterday. We will continue along the same path. In conclusion I would like to quote the opening words of Mr. Mazankowski's speech yesterday: "No new taxes. No tax increases". That is what we heard yesterday. Zero real growth in federal spending on programs and services. We will not spend more than in previous years.
It is the lowest federal program spending as a share of the economy in more than 30 years. Despite sometimes outlandish criticism of our budget, that budget stays the course Conservative budgets have followed since 1984, and it will guarantee a further economic recovery and economic expansion during the next five years.
That is why I am proud to be a member of this government and to take part in this debate on the budget. I hope we will hear at least a few positive comments from the opposition, and I also hope that some opposition members will give the government credit for what it has done and vote in favour of a status quo for government spending and against tax increases for this year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could the hon. member for Levis explain to me how he can be so proud of the financial policy of his government when, on page 15 of the budget, the Minister of Finance tells us that, even in 1998, the Canadian economy will not have regained its full production potential?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the opposition, member for his question. I will take this opportunity to explain to him that, since 1984, international circumstances have definitely changed. More and more, every country of the world is living in a global context. We

April 27, 1993
The Budget
cannot say that the situation was exactly the same in the previous decade.
We must take this global change into account. Also in the last few years, we went through a period where the Canadian economy experienced some depression caused, among other things, by external factors which led to some stagnation in our industrial process, the production process, and that definitely delayed some tax revenues.
That gave us additional challenges. We asked ourselves at one point if it was better to print money and reduce its value. We decided to go on the same road of restraint, and some are claiming that we are still going in the right direction, although the goal is a little farther away. This claim is shared by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, which comprises 24 European countries, by the International Monetary Fund, and mainly by the holders of Canadian bonds, the foreigners who are holding the Canadians' debt totalling more or less $275 billion. Those people must continue to believe in our fiscal policies and as a result of the budget, they do.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this budget debate. I want to concentrate particularly on one portion of it, which I view as an olive branch being offered by the Minister of Finance to his provincial counterparts. That olive branch involves the transfer payments that are made by the federal government to the provinces in the form of cash and tax points.
These transfers come by way of three programs: equalization, the Established Programs Financing and the Canada Assistance Plan. The budget indicates the intention to continue these major transfers to the provinces to the point where they will grow by 4 per cent over the next five years. The provinces will receive about $9 billion more than they would if these transfers were restrained to the same rate of growth as all other federal program spending, about 1.5 per cent.
For a province like Newfoundland, for example, allowing this higher growth rate in transfers means over $400 million more. That is almost twice the size of Newfoundland's deficit this year and is equal to $700 for each resident of that province.
I think this is an important gesture by the Minister of Finance and I commend him for it. He is recognizing that there is only one taxpayer. Whether we are talking about the municipal governments and their funding requirements, provincial governments or the federal government, at the end of the day all of these governments have only one source of funds and that is you, Mr. Speaker, me and other Canadians: the taxpayers.
For the past eight and a half years the federal government here in Ottawa has waged a lonely war against the deficit and the debt. The national debt was something like $207 billion in March 1985 at the end of the last year of the Liberal administration that was characterized by chronic overspending on programs and the constant building up of debt. That Trudeau-Chretien administration left behind a situation which has been very difficult for government to cope with ever since.
I think that it has been made more difficult by the distinct lack of federal-provincial co-operation. Before I touch on that I want to point out that as early as November 1984 this government began to address the problems. The Minister of Finance at that time said in his economic statement: "This government is prepared to lead this process of economic renewal. We have set for ourselves four challenges." First and foremost among those was: "to put our own fiscal house in order so that we can limit and ultimately reverse the massive buildup in public debt and the damaging impact this has on confidence and growth."
He went on to say that because he believed deficit reduction is the key to rebuilding confidence and confidence is the key to growth and job creation: "Controlling the deficit must be our priority for this year and for each year of our mandate. The goals of deficit control and increasing job opportunities cannot be separated."
That was Hansard, November 8, 1984. That has been the policy and position of the federal government ever since. I am happy to say we have made steady, solid progress. However, it has not been without difficulty because while we expected every single revenue-increasing measure and every single spending cut and program
April 27, 1993

curtailment to be opposed by the opposition parties in this House, we also found there are difficulties at the provincial level. There is duplication of bureaucracy and overlap in a number of areas such as forestry, mining, tourism, recreation and others where both levels of government are trying to function.
We have seen a disastrous failure to harmonize sales taxes. A simple harmonization of the GST and the provincial sales taxes would assist in administration, reduce bureaucracy, improve border control possibilities and provide a much needed boost for the small business sector because it would relieve it of having to pay tax on production input costs.
We have seen the destruction of some very valuable federal-provincial programs unilaterally. I cite for example the gross revenue insurance program. The federal-provincial agricultural support program was unilaterally gutted last year by the province of Saskatchewan.
We have seen along the way the imposition of provincial payroll taxes. One cannot help but suspect in some cases that the target is the federal payroll, especially in a province like Ontario. We have seen situations where the federal government has attempted to provide some tax relief by reducing income tax. However, as soon as the space was left open it was more than filled by provincial government tax increases, so we have countless examples of frustration and counterproductive activity.
Just two years ago the provincial government of Ontario, the Bob Rae administration, announced to the world that it was going to spend its way out of recession. This was after six and a half years of the federal government doing everything in its power to bring the spending scenario under control and get the deficit in line. Because it was in a deep hole, the Rae government decided it was going to dig the hole deeper and somehow this would solve the problem. Of course that has been shown to be nonsense. It could not help but frustrate the general direction in which the federal government has been attempting to steer the country. That is why I am pleased with the signal the Minister of Finance has given.
I want to say a little bit about off-loading. So often provinces give federal off-loading as their excuse for
The Budget
some of their problems, suggesting the federal government has cut or reduced its levels of transfers to the provinces. That in fact is not so. I found a very interesting editorial in the Globe and Mail of Wednesday, March 24 1993, headed "The facts about off-loading." I would like to quote from it because it sets out very succinctly the new age of enlightenment. It begins by saying: "Now that provincial governments of every political stripe have more or less admitted that the federal government was right all along about the dangers of deficit spending and that they were wrong, we trust they will also confess their error in the ongoing dispute over federal transfer payments."
The editorial goes on to mention the three systems of federal-provincial transfers. It points out that since 1986 the federal government has progressively cut the rate of growth in those payments, eventually freezing them in per capita terms. Since 1984-85 federal transfers to the provinces have increased from $24.6 billion to about $40 billion this year, a 60 per cent increase or about 6 per cent per year. While it may not be enough for the provinces, it is certainly more than other parts of Ottawa's budget received.
It concludes by saying: "No doubt the provinces were disappointed that Ottawa did not increase its transfers quite as fast as they, the provinces, were raising taxes at home, but the only reason that has been a problem for them is that their spending went on rising as if it had. But Ottawa could hardly have been expected to match the provinces in whatever absurd flights of spending they chose to take. If the provinces now find they have flown too high, it is not the fault of Ottawa for clipping their wings."
We have the situation where the provinces that have had the sole responsibility for education and health for many years let the spending run wild, failed to control it and then tried to upload their problems to the federal government.
The Minister of Finance has made a very important overture in this budget by agreeing to continue the increase in these transfer payments to the provinces. It is a very big ticket item for the federal government which it could very easily cut to reach an earlier balancing of the books and elimination of the federal deficit.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
As an overture, as an olive branch and as a signal to the provinces, the Minister of Finance has made that significant concession in his budget. Apparently we are going to have a meeting of federal-provincial ministers toward the end of May. We can hopefully look forward to some constructive activity leading to more federal-provincial co-operation in dealing with this very difficult insidious problem.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia is serious when he says that this budget shows openness to the provinces. The member mentioned that the provinces receive payments for three programs, which are called established programs, namely funding for health and education, equalization and shared funding of social assistance. We are told that expenditures will rise 4 per cent in the next five years while government spending is limited to 1.5 per cent.
What programs are we talking about? We know very well that per capita spending on health and education is frozen. There is no 4 per cent increase there. We also know that there is a cap on equalization payments, so what will increase in the next few years? Basically welfare payments. Why? The reason is very simple: because unemployment will rise dramatically.
The federal government's spending on unemployment insurance rose from $12 billion to $19 billion in two years. That is certainly not a 1.5 per cent increase. Since few jobs are expected to be created, people who are on unemployment insurance today will be on welfare tomorrow. Since the federal government has to pay 50 per cent of that, federal transfers will increase 4 per cent on average, but spending on this will go up by 10, 12 and 15 per cent a year. The provinces will have to pay half, so their spending will go up 10, 12 and 15 per cent a year, while transfers for education and health will not increase at all because they are frozen. We know that in tough economic times, spending on education rises because people stay in school or university longer and spending on health also goes up. I would like the hon. member to explain to me how the federal government has made an overture to the provinces.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the hon. member's question. I remind him that at the end of the day there is only one taxpayer in this country. That holds true whether we are talking about programs and expenditures of the federal government here in Ottawa, the various provincial governments or the municipalities.
It is incumbent upon all levels of government to act responsibly because they are all facing exactly the same pressures. We have gone through a period beginning in the late 1960s where program spending began to exceed revenue. Unfortunately successive governments borrowed at that time instead of raising taxes to commence paying for those programs as a signal to the people of what the cost was. They put it on the credit card and unfortunately the time has now come where this vicious cycle of having to pay interest is compounded to the point where it is a very serious constraint on the abilities of all levels of government to be able to meet the expectations of Canadians.
It is abundantly clear that Canadians from one end of this country to the other are determined to see some progress being made to bring down this treadmill of debt. In fact all of our revenues do not have to be consumed by paying interest on past borrowings.
The hon. member makes reference to problems of unemployment. At this time, I believe employment in this country is approximately 200,000 below the all-time high.
I would remind him that we have been in a stubborn global recession. I remind him of the term global recession because all of the countries of the world have been caught up in this.
It is not a made-in-Canada recession the way the opposition would like to suggest. I can cite the state of California which has lost 700,000 jobs over the past few years as a result of global recession. It is certainly not a made-in-Canada thing.
The fact is that this recession has resulted in less revenue coming in than had been projected. That is unfortunate. What it has done is slowed down the time at which we reach the point where the annual deficit is eliminated. It has been put off for a few years.
April 27, 1993

I think we would have been there by about 1994. It is going to be a little bit later. The good news is that thanks to the deficit control measures of the government, thanks to the lower inflation that follows and the lower interest rates and to the free trade agreement, we do see job creation.
There have been 200,000 additional jobs created in this country since last August. For nine consecutive months, employment has increased in the country. I think that is proof positive that over the long run these policies of prudence are going to pay off.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to a budget presented by the Minister of Finance yesterday.
When Canadians await and anticipate a national budget from their national government, they expect quite legitimately that the government will produce a financial blueprint that will address not only their particular economic predicament but the economic reality facing our country.
It is very similar to when families sit down to do their household budgets with their needs and difficulties. They try to be realistic. Governments should be charged with the same responsibility.
From this very simple perspective this budget was an irresponsible cop-out. It was a cop-out because it ran from the challenges and difficulties that are facing the country and that it helped create in the first place.
As a result, it failed Canadians economically in a time of great economic need. Just when our country needed some confidence and hope to overcome these economic challenges we receive as an answer a lack-lustre, leaderless budget document.
There is much that can be said about this document, particularly what it failed to do. I will dwell on five essential areas.
First, this budget as described by government members themselves was a basically stay-the-course budget. I could understand if the course was well received by the country, if the economy was vibrant, if people were satisfied, if the nation felt buoyant and if we were in a time of economic vitality. Then I could understand staying the course and hopefully staying it for a number of years.
The course that this country has been on for the last number of years in my humble suggestion, and I think it
The Budget
is shared by a great number of Canadians across the country because of their own individual lots, has been a very painful course. It therefore speaks to new remedies, to a change of course and new ideas and new assumptions.
Things are not working for all too many Canadians. Is this document rooted in reality? Does this government know or care about the 1.5 million unemployed? Does it care about the three million on welfare? Does it care about the plant closings in my city of metropolitan Toronto? Does it care that confidence is down across the country?
Does the government care that poverty is up every single year since it was elected? Do those members know that in addition to a recession still very much on on the streets of Canada our country psychologically is going through a depression and a state of very much insecurity largely triggered as a result of broken economic dreams and aspirations? The line-ups at food banks are getting longer, not shorter. There were 75 million pounds of food delivered to Canadians through food banks last year.
Talk to businesses Mr. Speaker and they will tell you that the proverbial turning of the comer is a long distance away. This government says technically by definition the recession is over. Ask workers. Ask retailers. Ask restaurateurs. Ask manufacturers. Ask the various entities that make up our national economy. Ask them and then ask consumers if we are out of the recession.
This budget is going to stay the course. What does the budget do for that course? This government and everybody else says that small businesses and medium-sized firms are the engine of jobs and economic growth. There are three lines about small business in this budget: "We increased already our substantial support for small businesses, the prime source of new job creation in Canada, and they are now creating jobs."
It talks about having created 200,000 full-time jobs over the last number of months. I would like to see where those jobs are. My city of metropolitan Toronto alone over the course of the last couple of years has assumed half of the job losses, over 230,000 jobs, of the entire country. It wants credit for having created, unsubstantiated in this document, 200,000 jobs.

April 27, 1993
The Budget
Where is the plan, where is the commitment, to finding a new course, a better course, a course that will work for more Canadians and not fewer? Let us abandon the stay the course mentality rather than applaud it.
Point number two, the foundations of this budget are based not on fact and action but rather the foundations of this budget are built on future projections and predictions.
As far as predictions go, all their past predictions about job creation and deficit reduction have been off base. For instance we pointed out today during Question Period that their projections for the deficit for this year were only off $8 billion. They assumed a debt of $148 billion. We are now up to $450 billion.
The second thing about predictions is that they predict in two, three, and five-year cycles. A very courageous government, is it not? Not that it will have anything to say about that particular part of Canada's future because it is going to be on this side after the next election. What does that say to Canadians who live in the here and now, Canadians who are unemployed today, students who do not have jobs today? They are saying: "Who cares what you predict about jobs in 1998 when I do not have a job today when you promised me two years ago that x amount of jobs would be created."
Look what it says about job prediction. Page 14 of the budget: "Job prospects will improve. I expect," the minister says, "employment to increase by about 300,000 jobs this year," can you imagine, "and next year more than 400,000 jobs."
Nowhere does it say how or where these jobs will be created. Predictions, projections, not much comfort for people who live with that economic malaise today and who know that unless things improve, when they wake up tomorrow morning that same malaise will be facing them once again. They know what this government can do with its predictions and projections. In the first words of the budget, the minister said there would be no new taxes or tax increases, and all of them applauded.
Canadians are not stupid. Canadians do not need to be offended anymore. Canadians know that since 1984 when this government regrettably took office there have been 36 different and new tax increases, including the GST. Canadians know the disposable amount of cash in
their pockets at the end of the month when they add up the federal, provincial and property taxes at the local level. This government now wants applause because after 36 tax hits it says maybe you deserve a break today. Then it asks why people have lost confidence in their government and institutions.
On point number three, where is the budgetary recipe for economic growth in this country? How will we increase jobs which will increase consumer spending, increase available amounts of cash or disposable income, increase confidence, increase demand, increase production, which will in turn increase government revenues and therefore pay for the services and programs that we have come to admire?
We all have to be fiscally responsible. This government, despite playing smoke and mirrors with the debt and the deficit and cutting has opted perceptionally to cut, cut, cut. How do you address the need to expand the economy and help it become more vibrant? You just cannot do it by cutting and slashing in the extreme and on its own. You cannot expand by constantly contracting. You can cut until you are blue in the face and have no heart left but it will still not speak to trying to expand and grow our economy and to try to make it work once again, rather than contracting, cutting and slashing. You need a balance when you are looking at a national economy. You just cannot hide under one fancy title that we are cutting, slashing and are responsible and the economy will respond to that. You need a balanced approach. Like all things in life you need to have a tempered balanced approach and our economy is no different.
For instance, we know that there is a capital cash crunch for small businesses and medium-sized firms. All of us, including the members on the government side, have said that is where job creation really is at its best. What does it say about helping the capital crunch, the credit crunch for those firms? Again three lines on page 5 and I quote:
In response to representations on the equity capital needs of smaller, knowledge-based firms, we will also explore ways to develop mechanisms to encourage investors to support local companies-
Explore, develop mechanisms, encourage-pap, after nine years. What has it said in terms of that credit crunch about banks? Banks were pulling back credit and freezing loans. Companies that for anywhere from 15 to 30
April 27, 1993

years had been good corporate clients of the major lending institutions could not get the time of day today.
Last Friday I had three calls in my constituency office. One was from a restaurateur, one from a food manufacturer and one from a small contractor. Each of them had been a client of the bank for over 15 years. Each of them had projects that would allow them to survive the drought. None of the three was able to get one dime from the chartered bank.
The story goes on and on. The banks have a role to play. I am not saying it is all their fault, not at all. I am saying that when looking at the equation of the national economy a very important variable is the role of the lending institutions. When there is a recession that role becomes doubly important.
Those banks should not be forcing small and mediumsized firms to pay for their lending mistakes to Campeau, O&Y or to South America. Those banks which exist because of entrepreneurship and risk taking should put their money where their mouths are. Take a risk with the small businessman. Allow him to refinance the truck. Take a risk and allow that restaurateur to expand and fill a new niche. Take a risk on that individual to buy a new piece of machinery that could perhaps do the job a little more effectively. Get behind some of those small and medium-sized firms.
We talked to the members of the Canadian Banking Association. When they visited our caucus I asked them of all the business loans portfolios to businesses what the percentage given to small and medium-sized firms was. After having told our caucus that is where the greatest number of jobs are created, less than 30 per cent of their business loans portfolio goes to small and medium-sized firms.
What does this government have to say about the role of our national lending institutions? That constituency is governed by federal statutes. As one important variable in that national economy they should be made to fulfil their role responsibly, not irresponsibly. If they fail to live up to legitimate lending practices that are needed for our times, well then it may be time for us as a Parliament and clearly as a government to revisit the
The Budget
statutes that give the banks the privileged place they enjoy in our country.
My fourth point is that the government keeps talking about the financial deficit. However, as a result of the dogmatic economic stay-the-course approach it has ignored the creation of a human deficit which manifests itself in different ways across our nation. There is a tremendous price to pay for those dogmatic stay-the-course economic policies when talking about a human deficit and sometimes we need to humanize the things we say or the policies that we create and pass.
How would you feel if you had to line up at a food bank for a piece of bread, Mr. Speaker? How would we feel if we had to go to an employment centre, only to see the same little cards indicating "thanks but no thanks" the day before? How would we feel if we were forced to live and exist off welfare? Think of the hurt and the stigma one would feel.
How would you feel if you were about to lose your job and what do you tell your family when you come home? How would you feel if you had to live below the poverty line? What hope would you derive the next day from this budget? What would you feel if you were part of the growing number of one-parent families led by single women, 60 per cent of whose jobs are below minimum wage? What confidence do you derive from this, if you are a senior and you are losing your house because you cannot afford to pay the property taxes after having sacrificed your entire life, or you are a young family and cannot afford to purchase that new house? How would you feel?
That is the human deficit members opposite prefer to ignore. Just like the chairman of the poverty subcommittee who pretends that the problems will go away if we raise the threshold of the poverty line. What insanity. What kind of blinkers are these men and women opposite wearing when they are oblivious to that human deficit? The tab keeps going up, not down. Let us look at that deficit while speaking rhetorically about the financial deficit.
This is my fifth and last point. Where is the inspiration that we are to be providing? When we talk about a budget we talk about inspiration and hope and not losing

April 27, 1993
The Budget
confidence. Where is that inspiration in this document that says we are going around the comer and together we are going to do it? There is none. There is no inspiration.
The leadership candidates on the other side condone the budget. Where is the newness? Where is the freshness? This really is the last chapter in a very sad Conservative tale. On top of it all, the Prime Minister has the audacity to spend $1 million on his egomaniac farewell tour when every other Canadian is left to make their own plan to get out of their economic misery. What a tale to finish this.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was an entertaining speech to say the least, but I think it has to be laced with a little reality. None of us could help but listen because it was a very forceful speech.
When the hon. member talked about some of the difficulties he saw in Canada and those aspects of the economy that none of us want to see, I think he ignored a great deal. That is the point I want to make. He ignored a certain amount of reality out there. We are talking about unemployment and about 1.5 million people unemployed. None of us can take much satisfaction in that. None of us can.
I would like to focus on the fact that Canada's economy is moving along nicely. Now it is not growing as fast as we would like it to, but certainly it is not a stagnant economy. It is not stagnant at all.
What we have to do is compare where Canada is today in relation to the rest of the world and it is not doing too badly. In fact the statistics indicate that Canada is doing better than the rest of the industrial world.
In fact the IMF predicts that Canada's growth rates of 3.2 per cent in 1993 and 4.4 per cent in 1994 will lead the rest of the world. One might ask why. It goes back to one of the statements the hon. member made. I will give the answer and the member can respond.
What he was saying in his speech was: "Listen, we can see the Draconian things you are doing in terms of cutbacks and trying to control the deficit." I accept that, but he asks as to what we are doing to enhance the growth of the economy. The words he used were: "What is the recipe that you are proposing? Show us in terms of what the minister delivered yesterday. Show us the recipe in that speech."
The recipe is indeed there. Let me point it out: low interest rates, the lowest interest rates we have seen in 30 years; the lowest inflation we have seen in this country in 30 years; and investment opportunity, the likes of which we have not seen in 30 years. Therein lies the recipe.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member says I am ignoring reality. The federal budget has two lines on jobs, zero lines on growth, two lines on small business and nothing about the banks. The hon. member talks about low interest rates, low inflation and great investment.
No one is investing in my province of Ontario. They are going to Dallas and Fort Worth, Texas and Phoenix, Arizona. Low interest rates and low inflation are academic issues because many people do not have jobs. The interest rates could be at 2 per cent but if you are not working, Mr. Speaker, you cannot invest. You cannot buy the cottage. You cannot buy the home, nor would you because you feel very insecure.
In terms of international comparison the hon. member takes great pride in saying: "Well we are going to lead the G-7 in terms of growth." He does not tell Canadians, nor does the Prime Minister, that of all the G-7 countries, we fell the furthest. Of all the G-7 countries our performance was the worst. Despite having dropped the furthest, our rebound according to economics is still not at the level it should be for the depths to which this government has brought this nation.
When the hon. member says that we are going to lead the G-7 countries out of the recession, why not also be honest and mention how deep the government brought this country down and that we were number one in terms of the worst economic performances.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment my colleague on an inspirational speech and especially the fact that he put so much focus on small business. We on this side of the House have been saying for the last two and a half years that the greatest hope for new job creation lies with the small business sector in this country. All the larger corporations are downsizing and dismantling. It is just an awful condition.
The thing that really disturbs me is the action the government took last December in its economic state-
April 27, 1993

ment. In that economic statement it amended the Small Businesses Loans Act. When we came back in February we all worked together to put that act through the House of Commons in record time. We as Liberals stood up and complimented the government, but we did it with one condition, that the Government of Canada would promote the Small Businesses Loans Act in every region of this country and that it would also call in the financial institutions and get them to get into the act.
We can have all these posters at the banks reading: "Low interest loans at 5 per cent or 6 per cent," but if the banks are not going to lend money then what good is it? It is almost like false advertising.
My question to my colleague is a tough one and I have tried to figure this out. What are we going to do to get the banking institutions of this country to wake up and realize that the small business community is crying out for help? Small businesses are our greatest hope for putting people back to work and they are not coming to the party.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from my colleague for Broadview-Greenwood. In his modest way he did not mention that for the last two and a half years he was very instrumental in trying to up the campaign of having all levels of government get behind our small and medium-sized firms and that great network of some 900,000 businesses across the country. If each of them were to create one or two jobs, imagine the type of stimulus we would derive.
I talked a bit about the banks. He talked about the small business loans. It really is a shell game unfortunately. When the government moved from the original $100,000 to $150,000 to the $250,000 small business development loans it would help underwrite, it was academic. Businesses in my riding told me that they could not even get to the first base of $100,000, never mind upping the threshold to $250,000. It was an attempt to try to suggest that somehow it was doing something great for the small business network.
What do we do with the banks? At the first opportunity, I think the first move should be one of co-operation. Have our chief financial lending institutions understand that their role in the national economy is a precious one, that during downturns it becomes doubly precious and
The Budget
that their variable is instrumental in the kind of output the economic equation gives us.
Second, if they are not prepared to have proper lending practices that reflect greater amounts of business loans to the small and medium-sized firms, which receive less than 30 per cent of all business loans from our banks, then we have to revisit the federal statutes that essentially give a monopoly for those chartered banks. I do not say that in a personal way and I do not say that in any nationalistic way. I only say it in order to add some muscle to the words we hear every single time we go back to our ridings.
The third area that I would mention is that of the chief inspector of the banks. I would like to put some teeth in that position to allow that inspector and the infrastructure around that office to actually take a look at those lending practices and see if they actually make sense with the times we are going through.
I would hope that we would first be able to sit down with the presidents of the major banks and lending institutions, which this government has not even begun to experiment with, and say that we are not putting the blame on them but the lenders must be engaged in a partnership in terms of stimulating and fomenting a more vibrant economy, taking risks and becoming the entrepreneurs they say that banks are founded on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first remark will be that this budget raises a simple question: why? I think that is the question that comes to the mind of many Canadians and Quebecers when they examine this budget, specially because this finance minister is probably more aware than any other Canadian of the seriousness of our fiscal problems in Canada.
If anybody is aware that strong action is urgently needed to regain control of our deficit and start paying off our debt, it is the present finance minister because the whole situation is known to him and he can get all the information, and because he is a member of a party and a government that was elected in 1984 on a platform that included putting our public finances in order. All Canadians remember that 1984 campaign when Conservative candidates travelled throughout Canada and Quebec telling everybody that the government should be

April 27, 1993
The Budget
replaced and how terrible the Trudeau government was because it had accumulated a $200 billion debt.
I remember vividly the comparisons that were used and the terror they stirred up in the public. People said, and rightly so, that that cancer had to be removed. They thought it was unbelievable that, in 10 years, we had gone from a more or less balanced budget to a national debt totalling $200 billion. That was one of the factors that helped the Conservatives beat the Liberals nine years ago. The Conservative government, with much stricter requirements with regards to fiscal balance and with a much healthier notion of public finances-at least that is what people thought-was elected on a restraint and recovery program. So nobody knows more than the present Minister of Finance how important it is to deal with a public debt that has jumped from $200 billion to close to $460 billion in nine years. He knows it so much that, in recent months, he was told by the IMF that we had to be careful, that Canada's debt and deficit situation was becoming dangerous. He himself did everything he could so that Canadians would be ready to accept extremely drastic measures in the budget.
Everybody in Canada knew that they would have to make sacrifices after this budget. Everybody was ready for that because the present Minister of Finance managed to convince Canadians that things were going wrong and that the government had to intervene. Virtually no analyst was expecting a mild budget.
However, as the minister knows, the Canadian debt is the second highest in the G-7. We know how this government reminded us, during the constitutional and referendum debates, that Canada belongs to this select club of the seven richest countries in the world. The fact is that Canada is the poorest of the richest countries in the world, or at least the most heavily in debt, second only to Italy.
The Minister of Finance is well aware of the situation, since he reminded us of the fact in the fiscal statement he delivered December 2. There was one important thing he told Canada which the insiders knew but the general public ignored. On page 40 of the background document included with the fiscal statement delivered on December 2, there is a chart showing Canada's international indebtedness.
People, especially government members, talk a lot about the magnitude of our debt, but seldom if ever about the honesty the minister of Finance showed last December, when he told us about the international indebtedness level of Canada.
It is important to note that Italy, whose debt is worse than ours, finances only 5 per cent of its debt on foreign markets. Foreigners account for only 5 per cent of Italy's debt. Otherwise, Italians borrow from Italians.
If the Italian government needs to borrow in order to pay its debt, which is higher than ours, then it borrows from Italian citizens. In Canada, when we need to finance our debt, which is the second highest in the G-7, we borrow at 40 per cent from foreigners. At least, that was the situation back in December, according to the chart provided by the Department of Finance, so, you see, I am not inventing anything, Mr. Speaker.
In matters of Canadian sovereignty, when speaking of Canada managing its own affairs, one has to remember that 40 per cent of the financial decisions concerning the debt are taken overseas. That is to say that Canada is essentially at the whim of the financial market and if by chance foreign creditors are not satisfied with anything we do, Canada is at risk and is left with no room to manoeuvre when managing the public finances, the affairs of this country.
If anyone knows how dangerous this situation is and how important it is to maintain a confidence level overseas so that these 40 per cent foreign creditors continue to extend financing to us, it is the minister of Finance.
And what does the Minister of Finance do? The time has come to present his last budget, the last of a series of nine budgets by this government that has received all the snubs and has had many trials and tribulations in the constitutional and economic areas, when he has finally the opportunity to really do something to solve a real problem, that is the public finances problem.
What does the Minister of Finance do? He presents a do nothing budget. Those who have commented on the budget today across the country, editorial writers and columnists alike, have all said that this is not a budget, that there is no budget here, no real measures to straighten the public finances, nothing to deal with the disastrous situation in Canada.
April 27, 1993

It is as if the Minister of Finance tried to avoid the necessary solutions. We all agree that it was not easy. We all recognize that there will not be a miracle and that the next Minister of Finance will have a lot to do to repair the mess he or she will inherit, that he or she will have to take continuous, aggressive and responsible actions to redress public finances. We all recognize that some decisions are difficult to take, but there are some which are less difficult to take.
For example, I cannot understand why this government did not decide to save money by eliminating waste and inefficiency that result from duplication of programs at the federal and provincial levels.
Recently, the members of the Quebec caucus of the Conservative Party presented to their colleague, the Minister of Finance, a paper in which they strongly recommended the transfer of the jurisdiction over manpower to the Quebec government. Everybody knows that if there is something that makes unanimity in Quebec, it is that transfer. People in the labour, business, cultural and political circles, the provincial Liberal Party and the Parti Quebecois, in short everybody in Quebec reached a consensus never seen before in asking that manpower training and development programs and policy-making be transferred to the Quebec government to make all the services accessible at a single window.
Instead of neutralizing each other's actions, instead of waging a war whose victims are the persons in need, those who lose their jobs or those whose jobs are at risk, let us create that single window everybody is asking for so we can meet the great challenges of our time.
All those people want single-window services in Quebec, including the Conservative caucus members from that province who, for once, did not hide to say this. They wrote it in a report published in the media. I think Senator Roch Bolduc and the hon. member for Joliette, Mr. Larrivee, are the leading figures who signed that report. The Tory members from Quebec also understood that this is an extraordinary way to stop wasting and to save, according to a Liberal minister from the Bourassa cabinet, some $250,000 a year right from the start. This is a lot of money in only one particular sector, and there are all the others.
The Budget
When he appeared before the Belanger-Campeau Commission, Pierre Fortin, a prominent economist, said that eliminating all duplication between Quebec and Ottawa could probably result in savings totalling up to $5 billion a year. There is one sector where duplication could have been eliminated very easily but it was not, even though everybody wanted that.
Mr. Speaker, whether you are federalist, sovereignist, Tory, Liberal or New Democrat, everybody in Quebec and in Canada knows that we will be the first generation who will pass on to the next one less than was ever passed on between generations in the history of Quebec and Canada. The building of a country is possible because a generation will pass on more than it has received. Slowly a real country is built and each generation passes on to the next one an invaluable heritage that it has enriched a little.
Our generation which perhaps received the most in history, in the whole string of transmissions, will be the first to pass on less than it received, to pass on a mortgaged country, a country that stifles the future of the rising generation, a polluted country, a country without a consensus. We are responsible.
We could have expected from this government that it would show courage, responsibility and some lucidity with respect to the present situation of those who are suffering and with respect to the future of those who justify our working, our struggling, that is our children and those who will come after them.
Moreover one would have thought that the Minister of Finance would spare himself this ridiculous exercise. He could have saved himself this touching exercise to help the two Tory Party leadership candidates save face because they ventured to make impossible and whimsical commitments when they said that if they took over from Mr. Mulroney as Prime Minister they would eliminate the deficit in five years. The Minister of Finance found it ridiculous. As one who for nine years has been part of a government that has been trying to reduce the deficit but only succeeded in increasing it to twice what it was before, he is the first to know that is impossible. He could not say it, but he could at least have kept quiet, but no, out of partisanship, out of electioneering solidarity, he wanted to help those two candidates that had ventured into the realm of ridicule and irresponsibility save face. He went through an exercise to prove that it could

April 27, 1993
The Budget
be reduced in five years. Indeed, he is saying that when he runs the country's finances, he can have a $32 billion deficit. However his successors will, through the workings of the Holy Spirit, or with the help of an extraordinary turn of events, reduce the deficit to $8 billion in five years, without tax hikes and cuts.
That is not the kind of Minister of Finance we are used to, especially since he indulged in unacceptable intellectual and accounting distortions. Does he not forecast in his budget that in certain years tax revenues will grow twice as fast as our economy, which does not make any sense? Any second-grade kid, who has learned basic arithmetic, knows on the face of it that it is a sham, but we must say that he tried that tack for his party's sake, so that the two poor candidates who said they would work miracles could save face.
After saying that I do not understand what happened, I could perhaps make an assumption, which in fact would explain the very existence of the Bloc Quebecois. First, how did the debt get so big? There are several reasons for it. Of course there are international and structural reasons, reasons related to problems with the economy throughout the world. We are not the only country in debt, but we are among the most indebted. To be sure, it is partly due to external factors and causes.
However a very large part is due to our inability to have a real consensus in this country. For a long time, the federal government threw money at problems in order to tighten its grip on the provinces and create a sort of fictitious Canadian unity. It paid to have duplicate institutions in the east and in the west. If someone somewhere clamoured, that person was paid off, and so it went. Rationality and efficiency were not the governing criteria most of the time or very often, but it was a way to buy peace.
Since Canada is tremendously rich in natural resources, we could go on paying for a long time, but when we no longer had the money required, we started to borrow. We borrowed so much that we can no longer do so now. We have reached the point where it is obvious that Canada cannot go on. This can be seen in the impossibility of finding a solution to the problem of the deficit.
There is a reason behind the Minister of Finance's inability to propose something that would straighten out the country's finances-it can be done, as we well know-in a fiscally responsible and socially just manner, by calling on everyone to accept some sacrifice, it can be done. The Americans will do it with President Clinton. It can be done in a country with a close sense of nationhood. Not here; it is not possible here to convince the east and the west to accept the same sacrifices. This is a country where an aircraft maintenance contract is enough to tear the country apart. A contract for helicopters or frigates is enough to tear the country apart. This is a country with no consensus.
The Canadian political structure does not correspond to reality. Our big problems like the budget and government finance require a fundamental solution. The problem is structural and the solution must be structural too. That is why we believe that since there are two realities in this country, two political, economic and social realities, there must be two political entities.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons and to Minister of National Defence):

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I was listening to the comments of my hon. friend from Lac-Saint-Jean concerning the budget some questions came to my mind.
First, the member for Lac-Saint-Jean, who was once a cabinet member in this government, must surely recall that, when the Conservative Party came to power in 1984-85, the debt was already very close to $200 billion and that this debt had mushroomed over a very short period of three or four years.
My hon. friend will also recall that the government's current account deficit was $16 billion. Let me briefly explain what we mean by the government's current account. It is simply the account into which go all revenues collected by the government through taxes- the income tax, excise taxes and other revenues-minus its operating expenditures. This current account was in the red to the tune of $16 billion, which means that the Governement of Canada was actually borrowing to pay for groceries.
In 1987-88 the member for Lac-Saint-Jean was a cabinet member. After the 1988 election, he realized that instead of a current account deficit, there was now a surplus. I think the member for Lac-Saint-Jean, as a
April 27, 1993

minister of the Crown, had also experienced cuts in his department's operating expenditures.
I remember perfectly when the member for Lac-Saint-Jean presented the green plan with a lot of money to spend. I remember how impatient he became several times when he could not get these sums of money, because this government and this finance minister remained responsible. He could not get all the money he wanted in spite of all the good things that were said about the green plan.
The member for Lac-Saint-Jean will probably recognize, as I do, that this government has tried consistently to put the public finances in order. The member for Lac-Saint-Jean is criticizing the Budget. Would he have agreed, and it is the first part of my question, if yesterday the finance minister had announced massive cuts to transfer payments to the provinces? Would he have agreed if the government had announced massive cuts to transfer payments to those who need them the most, that is the elderly, the handicapped, the veterans? Would he have agreed with that? I think that having been part of the government, he is in a position to realize that there are things that cannot be changed without jeopardizing the very economic structure of the country.
I will ask him a second question to give him the opportunity to answer. The member for Lac-Saint-Jean has recognized, or at least, stressed the fact that training programs should be transferred to the Quebec government. I think that a consensus is emerging on that. Could he tell us why last October he campaigned against the Charlottetown Accord according to which manpower training programs would have been entirely transferred to the Quebec government?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Manicouagan for these two questions. In response to his first question, I will have the opportunity to clarify once and for all the gossip peddled by government members, in particular the President of the Treasury Board when he goes to Chicoutimi and claims that the reason I broke ranks was that I was not given the money I had requested for the
The Budget
environment. I have written a rebuttal, but the minister never replied to that letter that I have had published.
As a matter of fact, I did get the money I had asked for. I wanted $5 billion to finance the green plan over a six-year period, and I got it. If the funding was later cut to $3 billion, I am not responsible for that. When I was minister, the funding for the green plan was $5 billion. It would have remained at $5 billion if I had stayed in office, because I fought for the environment. I believed that this government should do something positive for the environment, that it should make sure that we leave a clean, unpolluted country for future generations. Do not come and tell us today that we did not look after the environment. I insisted that we do so when I was in office, and we did.
Second, I want to deal with the hon. member's second question. It is obvious that, beyond the partisan sparring-and the quality of the debate has just gone down a notch but let us get back to the actual question being debated-the lack of consensus has been evident, especially since 1990 when the Bank of Canada had to use monetary policy as a club to impose interest rates that were obviously destructive for the economy of Quebec especially, and for the rest of Canada, except Ontario. Because the economy in Toronto was overheated as we must admit, the whole country had to take the drastic remedy of extremely high interest rates which had a direct impact on the interest the government itself owed its creditors. That literally killed business investment across Canada so that much of today's debt is actually due to the Bank of Canada's high interest rate policy, because this country cannot reach a consensus.
Just think that even today, the real interest rate in Canada is still double the real interest rate in the United States. That is not right. We are living next to the largest economy in the world, and we are separated from it only by a border, an imaginary line. Our economies are interrelated, integrated, as we well know; we are united by a free trade agreement. Why is it then that we need a real interest rate-that is, the mathematical interest rate minus the rate of inflation-twice as high as the American rate in order to protect the Canadian dollar? It is because this country has a political problem. Not an economic problem, a political one. The hon. member for Manicouagan is well aware of that. After all, he is from an area where the voters were overwhelmingly against the Charlottetown Accord he just referred to.

April 27, 1993
The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Lac-Saint-Jean takes great pleasure in defending jurisdictions. In this budget, if there is a sector where we could make drastic cuts, it is in the field of transfers to provinces. These transfers affect education, health, social services, et cetera.
I want to ask a question of the hon. member. Does he not think that it is preferable, as the Minister of Finance said in his speech, to first consult with provinces to arrive at a rational plan for reducing transfers to those provinces? The increases will be 4 per cent. Agreements have been signed and I think they must be complied with. Since the debt and the deficit are a national problem, it is important that all provincial governments reach an agreement with the federal regarding a reduction of expenditures in the field of transfers. This seems perfectly logical, while at the same time respectful of the provincial jurisdictions.
I will conclude by asking a second question to my colleague from Lac-Saint-Jean. We usually make judgments based on results. Since my colleague was the Canadian ambassador to Paris for three years, perhaps he could tell me which budget restrictions he implemented at the Canadian embassy in Paris, where several dozen employees work. I would also like to know if, in all conscience, he applied those budget restrictions objectively.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my natural modesty has always prevented me from reporting on my tight management of the embassy in Paris, but he will let me do so since he is forcing me to do it today.
I was the only ambassador in Europe at the time who suggested cutting the staff in his embassy to the Department of External Affairs. I voluntarily proposed a reduction plan before I was asked. If I am not mistaken, because it was some time ago, I believe that we cut about 20 positions in Paris. I thought that we were overstaffed and I cut about 20.
If people tell me that I did not run a tight ship in the embassy, I was the most highly rated ambassador in Europe at the time for my management, if, Mr. Speaker, you will allow me to boast, since the hon. member mentioned it.
Secondly, regarding transfers to the provinces, is the member for Chicoutimi saying that he would like the federal government, which picked up these tax points during and after the war and must now distribute them back to the provinces, not to do so anymore but to keep this money and continue to impose requirements on the management of social programs in Quebec by saying "If you charge user fees we will stop paying"? Is he telling us that he would like the federal government to withdraw completely from transfers to the provinces for education and social programs?
If so, what does a federal government do? It proves what we are saying: the federal government must be abolished, at least as far as Quebec is concerned. Quebec must become a sovereign country that will look after its own social affairs, education and the rest, without sending over $20 billion in tax payments to Ottawa.
The member for Chicoutimi is just saying what almost all his constituents want: a sovereign government in Quebec City.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in the budget debate. I think I will pick up where I left off when I questioned one of the members opposite with regard to their speech.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member indicate whether he will speak for 20 minutes or will split his time with another colleague?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going for the full 20 minutes and I guess that will give me some time for tomorrow's session as well.
Picking up where we left off in debate with the member opposite there is no question today about the direction from which the opposition is coming. Those members are attacking again where they left off and have left off consistently in terms of debate and their structure of the debate when it comes to the finances of the Government of Canada.
I was taken today by the remarks in the House by the Minister of Finance when he talked about the same line coming out of the lips of the members opposite. Basically when it is all sorted out they are not committed to deficit reduction at all. I think if their words are carefully measured over there on that side of the House then the
April 27, 1993

Minister of Finance is absolutely correct. They like to talk about deficit reduction but when push comes to shove they really just want to pay lip service to it. That has surfaced in their remarks continually today. As the minister stated today their words really do not go beyond this. It is spend, spend, spend, borrow, borrow, borrow and tax, tax, tax. That has been a very consistent theme today.
They have been making some headway in this debate. I want to clarify this and step through what we have done. When they go beyond deficit and get off the deficit number then their argument simply is based on, for example, what one is doing to encourage investment in the economy. That is fair game and I think that is fair debate. I want to step through what we are doing because it is important to put it on the record.
What we are doing is pretty evident and it was evident in last year's economic statement which the minister brought down in December. That economic statement spoke pretty clearly in terms of what we are doing. Basically it comes down to this. The basic points of the argument are, and we have to mention this because it is very important the government do so, low interest rates, the lowest interest rates we have seen in this country for 20 years, almost 30 years, and low inflation rates, the lowest inflation rates we have seen in this country for 30 years. They are just part of the basics we have, but we also should fix firmly on crunching that deficit number.
That is where we have the basics right. That is where it is showing up in terms of investment in the Canadian economy. That is what we are doing. We are encouraging investment. We are encouraging growth in the economy.
I want to put on the record some remarks by the International Monetary Fund. The IMF sees Canada on a growth path. The evidence speaks pretty clearly for the Government of Canada in that regard. The IMF projects growth rates of 3.2 per cent for Canada in 1993 and 4.4 per cent in 1994.
What are those numbers really saying? They are saying that Canada is doing very well, thank you very much, in the face of the rest of the world. In other words, when we compare our economy to that of the United States or any economy in the western world, even countries like Japan,
The Budget
we are doing very well. The growth in the Canadian economy will exceed every one of the western European economies this year. As for the far east, we will exceed the growth of the Japanese economy as well. We have consistently done that as a nation since 1984. From 1984 to the present only one country in the hemisphere has exceeded Canada in terms of economic growth. Which is it? It is Japan.
We are doing fairly well, but not as good as I would like because 1.5 million unemployed people are too many for an industrialized country like Canada. We acknowledge that. We have to acknowledge it in the face of reality. We have to acknowledge what other countries are doing in comparison to us. They were caught in a world-wide recession as was Canada.
The members opposite say: yes, but the recession in Canada was worse. I agree it was worse. It was worse because our trading partners were going through that hurt as well. As a result of the fact that Canada is a trading nation we depend on the health of those other nations that buy products from us. Evidence of that, in terms of what we produce and sell to the rest of the world, is very compelling.
Last year Canada exported $157 billion worth of goods to the rest of the world. It was a remarkable turnaround for Canada. As the economies of the United States and western Europe started to speed up they were paying net dividends into Canada's economy. It takes a while for that to work through the economy. If they are buying $157 billion worth of goods from us today it does not mean that all the factories are up and running tomorrow because it does take time to work through the system. However, believe me it is happening.
Some of the numbers indicate that it is happening. Those numbers that have been put out by the International Monetary Fund are pretty clear evidence that it is working. Our economic policies are starting to work. Why? They are starting to work because our companies will invest in economies where there is security. They will invest where there is security.
When they look at Canada they will say: "Listen, your interest rates are the lowest they have been in 20 years. I like that. I think I will invest in Canada. Inflation is the

April 27, 1993

lowest it has been in 20 or 30 years. I like that. I am going to invest." They have and it is paying dividends for us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is scary.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member opposite says: "It is scary." The only thing scary in the House is the thought of that party coming over here and governing us again.
Now that he has mentioned the word scary, I have some numbers here which are pretty scary. We always talk about the combined debt in this country and where it came from, how we arrived at this huge mountain of debt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Here we go, the 10-year old story.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a 10-year old story and I think it has to be put on the record very clearly. I have done it on a number of occasions and I will continue to do it.
I want to mention some of the difficulties we inherited as a government. I am not going to prolong the agony. Between 1968 and 1984, and incidentally those where the years when Pierre Trudeau was the Prime Minister of Canada, he took the country from a zero deficit position to a deficit of $32 billion. When we are talking about the deficit, just to remind the folks back home, the deficit is a yearly number. That is the amount by which the Government of Canada overspends on a yearly basis. He took it from a zero position-in other words in 1967-68 it was a balanced budget-up to the point where they were borrowing $32 billion a year to pay their bills.
What is really astonishing about that is that when they left office in 1984 the gross domestic product of Canada was just slightly over $400 billion. Today it is around $700 billion. That is just an example of running up a deficit of $32 billion in 1984, and there were revenues of only $71 billion.
By way of passing, our revenues this year will be somewhere around $122 billion to $125 billion, and the economy is around $700 billion. Remarkably we have kept our deficit down to that $35 billion number.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the debt?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The combined debt. When any government inherits a yearly deficit of $32 billion and the government of the day in 1984 was spending $1.33 on programs for every dollar it took in the door, it is in a very difficult position with regard to cash flow.
Today we have-and I know they take a great deal of pleasure in this-a combined debt of over $400 billion in which none of us can take any pleasure because it has doubled.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: $450 billion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member opposite says: "$450 billion." It is not quite $450 billion. The exact number as we speak is around $416 billion. Again, it is not a number any of us can take pride in.
From 1984 to the present day the combined debt of the country has doubled. What they do not like to talk about is the stranglehold they had on the government, that is the previous government when it left office. They put us in a cash crunch situation.
The hon. member opposite chuckles. The point I would like to make is that between 1968 and 1984 the debt did not double under their government. The debt increased 10 times; it increased tenfold. We are guilty of doubling it and we accept that. However, it is the compound interest on the debt we inherited. We have not put one single nickel on to that debt load. It is all combined interest. It is the killing effect of compound interest on a debt that we inherited.
Let us go beyond that because it is an old story. Nobody wants to talk about it anymore, especially the opposition. How do we get beyond that? The minister told us yesterday to get beyond that by encouraging investment and not stifling it. We cannot stifle investment because if we do we are going to kill the economy. We must have a balance.
We on this side of the House acknowledge that we cannot do it. In other words we cannot pay off the debt simply by taxing Canadians more because there is not a single Canadian out there who is going to buy into that idea. I am one of them.
If we cannot tax the folks any more, and I think most of us would argue that we cannot, what do we do? We can
April 27, 1993

do a number of things. We can encourage investment, which we are doing. We can encourage growth in the economy which is happening and that is good.
We can also reduce the cost of government and size of government. That is something we have done consistently since taking office in 1984. We have reduced the cost of government, the size of government. On every single measure in every budget that we brought into this House to do that, the opposition consistently voted against it.
What it comes down to is talking out of both sides of your mouth on any particular issue because when you are elected, you do. Your feet in a sense I suppose are held to the fire because that is the price of governing.
The price of governing is making those tough decisions. They do not make you particularly popular with the folks back home or in the polls but at the end of the day the government of the day has to make the tough decisions and we have made those, made them consistently and they are starting to pay off.
Before I sit down I want to talk about the budget and who it has impacted on in terms of the cost of doing business or the reduction in the size of government and government spending. Who has it impacted on?
I am very proud to say we did not touch any of the social programs in yesterday's announcement. The minister as he stepped through the budget papers indicated that there are going to be total savings in this package of approximately $30 billion in the next four years.
We did not touch seniors or their pensions. We did not touch any of the support payments for veterans. We did not touch any of those programs which are important to a province like my home province of New Brunswick. We did not touch transfers to the provinces. In fact the growth of the transfers, the federal dollars to the provinces is going to grow, particularly for the poorer provinces like my home province of New Brunswick.
Why is that important to me? The province of New Brunswick depends on 40 per cent of its revenues from the Government of Canada. This year that will amount to about $1.5 billion. Obviously a small province like New Brunswick cannot afford to lose $1.5 billion. The good news is that it will not. That is extremely good news for the provinces back east.
Government Orders
To sum up, Canadians want to see an end to the deficit and they want to see it achieved through spending cuts and growth in the economy. They do not want to see it through higher taxes.
When those folks get up across the way and pretend to be in favour of tightening up government, reducing the cost and the size of the government, listen very carefully to what they are saying. At the end of the day I am reminded by the words of the finance minister today in the House during Question Period. If we sort out everything they say it basically comes down to the same three words: spend, borrow and tax.
The Canadian people have had it with taxes. They have had it with borrowing and they have had it with spending.
